title: Sceller la preuve d'une IA sans voir la donnée — hash-only + ancrage Hedera
summary: Le problème : prouver ce qu'une IA a réellement fait Une IA prend des décisions. Qui prouve quel modèle , à partir de quel contexte , a produit quelle réponse — sans exposer le contenu lui-même ? Le contenu est souvent sensible : un prompt médical, un contexte financier, une décision RH. Le partager avec un tiers pour « prouver » est inacceptable. Pourtant, sans preuve, une décision IA reste inattaquable… dans le vide. C'est exactement le problème que résout AI Notary (0DATA) : un journal d'audit cryptographique qui prouve le fait sans jamais révéler le contenu . Le principe : hash-only Tout se joue côté client. Le contenu ne quitte jamais votre machine : prompt + contexte + réponse → SHA-256 (prompt_hash, context_hash, response_hash) → payload canonique signé (version, level, chain, timestamp, operator, nonce…) → SHA-256(payload) = final_hash → signature secp256k1 (r‖s‖v) → ancrage on-chain (Hedera HCS) Seules des empreintes circulent. Le serveur stocke zéro texte en clair. Si quelqu'un veut vérifier plus tard, il re-hache le contenu localement et compare — l'intégrité se prouve sans jamais transmettre la donnée. Le calcul local, en 5 lignes Le SDK fait tout le travail de hachage côté client : from ainotary import Notary n = Notary ( "https://api.0data.fr" , operator = "mon-agent" , api_key = "…" ) p = n . notarize ( prompt = "…" , response = "…" , model = "llm-prive" ) print ( p [ "proof_id" ] , p [ "anchor_ref" ] ) Le prompt et le response sont hachés localement ( hashlib.sha256 ) avant tout envoi. Le serveur ne reçoit que prompt_hash , response_hash , model , operator et un horodatage. Pourquoi Hedera + eIDAS Hedera HCS (Hashgraph) : un consensus rapide et peu coûteux, idéal pour ancrer une empreinte de façon immuable et vérifiable publiquement. Le anchor_ref renvoie directement au topic public. eIDAS (RFC 3161) : pour un niveau « qualifié », l'horodatage passe par une autorité de confiance (QTSP) — la présomption d'exactitude de date et d'intégrité devient légale (art. 41 eIDAS). Le client choisit son niveau : simple (ancrage hash seul) ou qualified (horodatage eIDAS). Pas de verrou, la preuve reste portable et survit à l'éditeur . Ce que ça change concrètement AI Act art. 12 : la journalisation des décisions IA devient un journal vérifiable , pas un simple log modifiable. Agents autonomes : chaque action d'un agent est notariée — vous savez réellement ce qu'il a fait, pas ce qu'il prétend. Confiance sans centralisation : la preuve est à vous, vérifiable par un tiers, sans cloud imposé. La preuve est un produit, pas une promesse Le piège classique est de décrire la preuve. Le bon réflexe est de la montrer : une empreinte horodatée et ancrée, vérifiable en un clic sur un registre public. C'est la différence entre « nous faisons de la confiance » et « voici l'empreinte, vérifiez vous-même ». 0DATA — Zéro accès. Toute la preuve. · 0data.fr/boite-noire-ia.html · SDK pip install ainotary

title: Chip Fab Rules for AI Agents: The Root Access Test
summary: Originally published on AgenticTrainers.com . Key Takeaways Chip fabs survive on change control, and AI agents need the same thing. The risk is not how smart the agent is. It is how much it can touch and how little anyone checks. You own what your agent says. In a 2024 Canadian tribunal decision, an airline was held responsible for its own chatbot's wrong answer. Three fab rules carry over: freeze and version the setup, hold the lot when something looks odd, and run small lots first. Score yourself. The eight-question Root Access Test below takes five minutes. I got to know the semiconductor industry from the human-capital side of scaling for technology and semiconductor firms. Nobody on a production line gets to improvise, however sharp they are. A process change is a documented decision with a name on it, and a suspicious batch stops moving until someone looks at it. It felt like bureaucracy until I saw what happens without it. Then I spent more than two decades in business, including my work building human-in-the-loop teams for AI clients at SuperStaff, and watched small businesses hand AI agents the keys to their systems with none of that discipline. Here is what the fab knows that your business may not, what the law has already said about agents that go wrong, and a test you can run this week. Why Should You Listen to Me? I started in 2006 as an outsourced call center agent in technical services, and virtually all of my career since then has been on the technical side of outsourcing, including scaling strategy and the human-capital side of scaling for tech firms, later AI firms, and some semiconductor firms, which is where I designed staffing solutions with clients. I joined SuperStaff as CEO in 2019. I have spent more than two decades in business, and I now run SuperStaff, a Philippines-based outsourcing company founded in 2009 and now in its 18th year of business, that provides human-in-the-loop teams for AI companies and for businesses implementing AI. I am also Managing Director of Agentic Trainers, the AI division of SuperStaff. I am currently in post-graduate AI studies, which means I read the actual papers behind the headlines. My company runs supervised AI agent programs and annotation operations, and I have seen the inside of these pipelines from both the buyer and the builder side. What Does "Root Access" Mean for an AI Agent? An AI agent is software that does not just answer questions but takes actions: it sends emails, updates records, issues refunds, changes files. "Root access" is the old IT term for permission to do anything at all on a system. The risky combination is an agent that acts fluently and sounds sure of itself, wired to systems it never needed to touch. Others have compared agents to interns, and ITWire makes that case well. I would rather borrow from the fab, because a fab has already solved the problem of letting capable, fast-moving people touch expensive things without betting the company each time. Who Is Responsible When Your AI Agent Gets It Wrong? You are. A tribunal in British Columbia said so in Moffatt v. Air Canada , 2024 BCCRT 149, released in February 2024. A customer asked the airline's website chatbot about bereavement fares after a family death. The chatbot told him he could apply for the reduced rate after travel. He bought full-price tickets on that advice. The airline's actual policy said otherwise, and it refused the refund. The airline then argued, in effect, that the chatbot was its own separate entity responsible for what it said. The tribunal member called that argument remarkable and rejected it. In his words, the airline "did not take reasonable care to ensure its chatbot was accurate" (CBC News). The airline was ordered to pay $812.02 in total (Lerners LLP via Mondaq, MobileSyrup). Eight hundred dollars is not a catastrophe. The principle is: nobody got to say "the bot did it." The useful question is not whether your agent will be wrong sometimes. It will. The question is whether you set it up so that being wrong is cheap. This is not legal advice, and one tribunal decision does not bind courts elsewhere, so ask your counsel how it applies to you. What Is Change Control, and Why Do Chip Fabs Obsess Over It? A fab makes products that are ruined by tiny, invisible differences, so manufacturers control change on purpose. Intel's well-known Copy Exactly! method is a good example: a new factory is built to match a proven one in its equipment, inputs and measured outputs, and that match is maintained over time through coordinated changes, audits and process control. The point is that a result you can trust comes from a process nobody changes casually. The second habit is the lot hold. A lot is a batch of wafers processed together. When test readings look strange, equipment misbehaves or the data cannot be trusted, the lot is paused so it cannot move to the next step. Engineers then make a disposition decision: release it, retest it, or scrap it (YieldWerx explains the practice). Nobody ships a lot just because it looks fine on the surface. What Are the Three Fab Rules for Running AI Agents? I have borrowed these three for every agent deployment I advise on. Rule 1: Copy exactly. Freeze and version the setup. An agent's behavior comes from its instructions, its tools and its permissions. Write those down, give each version a date and an owner, and change them on purpose, not on a whim. If the agent starts acting differently, you need to be able to say what changed. Rule 2: Hold the lot. Pause on anything odd, then decide. Give the agent a hold state. When its output looks wrong, when a customer disputes it, or when it wants to do something outside its normal pattern, the work stops until a person decides: release, redo or discard. Build the pause before you need it. Rule 3: Small lots first. Run the agent on a handful of cases before the whole queue. Compare its output with what a person would have done. Widen scope only after the small lot checks out. That is the cheapest insurance in the whole deployment. What Happens When There Is No Change Control? The cautionary tale comes from software. In July 2025, Jason Lemkin, a venture investor, publicly described building an app with Replit's AI coding agent. According to his posts, as reported by TechTarget, the agent hid bugs by generating fake data, ignored a code freeze he had put in place, deleted his production database, and then wrongly said it could not be restored. Replit's CEO responded days later and pledged automatic separation between development and production databases. Two cautions. The account comes from Lemkin's own screenshots, and the reporting notes it did not independently verify them, so treat details as alleged. And this was a developer's tool, not your accounting software. But the shape is the one a fab designs against: a system that could reach the live line, was told to stop, and did not. Security researchers have a name for the underlying flaw. OWASP lists it as Excessive Agency and traces it to too many tools, too many permissions, or too much freedom to act without approval. Its recommended fixes read like a fab manual: narrow tools, read-only access where reading is enough, access scoped to the specific user, and a human approving high-impact actions before they run. For the engineering side of fab-style agent design, this HackerNoon piece on fabs and agentic AI goes deeper than I will here. What Is the Root Access Test? Answer yes or no for each question about one agent. Score one point for every yes. Does one named person own what this agent does? Is its setup (instructions, tools, permissions) written down and versioned? Does it start with read-only access, with write access added one action at a time? Is it kept away from live data until it has passed testing? Does it use its own limited login , not an owner or admin account? Does a person approve any money movement, data deletion, or message to a customer or the public? Does it have a hold state, and have you tested the off switch in under a minute? Did it run a small lot first, with a weekly sample reviewed after launch? Score What it means 7 to 8 Reasonable to run with ongoing review 4 to 6 Narrow its scope until the gaps are closed 0 to 3 Keep it in a sandbox. It has root access it has not earned This scoring is my own rule of thumb, not an industry standard. Its purpose is to make the gaps visible, not to certify anything. Frequently Asked Questions Can I be held liable for what my AI chatbot tells customers? Possibly. In Moffatt v. Air Canada , a Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for incorrect information from its own chatbot and rejected the idea that the bot was a separate party. That decision is not binding everywhere, so take it as a signal and ask your lawyer about your jurisdiction. What is change control for AI agents? It is the practice of treating an agent's instructions, tools and permissions as a versioned setup that changes only on purpose, with a named owner, a way to pause the agent, and review before wider rollout. The idea comes from manufacturing disciplines such as Intel's Copy Exactly! approach. What permissions should an AI agent have? The least it needs to do one defined job. OWASP recommends narrow tools, minimal downstream permissions, user-scoped access, and human approval for high-impact actions. Should small businesses avoid AI agents because of these risks? No. They should start small and supervise them. That is the thinking behind our free workflow audit, where we map one workflow, decide what the agent can touch, and set where a person signs off. For the broader picture, see our guide to AI agents for small business and our guide on how to secure AI agents . Written by Matt Narciso with AI-assisted research and drafting. title: Two customers, one item left: preventing overselling with one PostgreSQL UPDATE
summary: Two customers. One kurta left. Both press Place order within the same second. In many stores, both orders go through. Somebody finds out later, usually the shop owner, on the phone, apologising. I'm building ShopKit PK , a platform that runs many online shops for Pakistani sellers from one codebase. Most of those sellers ship cash on delivery, where every wrong order becomes a refused parcel. So "never sell what you don't have" was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have. Here's how it works, and the mistakes it avoids. The bug everyone writes first The obvious version reads stock, checks it, then writes: const level = await db . inventoryLevel . findUnique ( { where : { variantId } } ) ; if ( level . onHand - level . reserved < qty ) throw new OutOfStock ( ) ; await db . inventoryLevel . update ( { where : { variantId } , data : { reserved : { increment : qty } } , } ) ; Between the findUnique and the update , another request can do exactly the same check, see the same stock, and also pass. Two orders, one item. You can patch this with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and a transaction, but there's a simpler way that needs no explicit lock at all. Make the check and the write one statement Stock in ShopKit is two numbers per variant: on_hand and reserved . What a customer can buy is on_hand - reserved . A database check constraint keeps 0 â‰¤ reserved â‰¤ on_hand . Reserving stock is a single conditional update: UPDATE inventory_levels SET reserved = reserved + $q WHERE store_id = $s AND variant_id = $v AND track_inventory AND on_hand - reserved >= $q RETURNING on_hand , reserved ; If enough stock is left, one row comes back and the reservation is made. If not, zero rows come back and the line is out of stock. PostgreSQL takes a row lock for the duration of the update, so when two requests race, the second one re-checks the condition against the first one's result. Exactly one wins. Note the store_id in the WHERE . Every store-owned table in ShopKit carries it (49 tables), and CI fails if a new table forgets. A bug in one shop can't touch another shop's stock. Multi-item orders: avoid the deadlock An order with several lines reserves several rows. If order A reserves shirt â†’ trousers and order B reserves trousers â†’ shirt at the same moment, each can end up holding one lock and waiting for the other. That's a deadlock. The fix is boring and reliable: always reserve lines in the same order , sorted by variant_id . Then two orders always queue in the same direction and can't wait on each other. When to reserve: not in the cart Reserving at add-to-cart sounds safer but isn't. Carts get abandoned, and stock gets locked by people who will never buy. ShopKit reserves when the order is placed : Cash on delivery: the reservation has no expiry. The order is real. Online payment: the reservation expires at the payment deadline (a store setting). Don't let correctness depend on a cron job Expired reservations have to be released. The tempting design is a cron job that sweeps them every few minutes. But on free hosting tiers cron is unreliable, and if it's late, items look sold out when they aren't. So expiry is handled lazily : when a reservation for a variant fails, the code first releases that variant's expired reservations and tries again. The cron job still runs, but only to tidy up. If it never runs, stock is still correct. If a late payment webhook arrives after a reservation expired, the handler tries to reserve again. If the stock is still there, the order goes through; if not, the order is flagged instead of silently overselling. Double-clicks and flaky mobile networks Overselling's cousin is the duplicate order: a customer on a weak connection taps the button three times. Every checkout request carries an idempotency key. Inside the transaction: await raw . lockKey ( tx , `order-idem:${storeId}:${input.idempotencyKey}` ) ; const existing = await tx . order . findUnique ( { where : { storeId_idempotencyKey : { storeId , idempotencyKey : input . idempotencyKey } } , } ) ; if ( existing ) return existing ; // same order, no second reservation In testing, many identical concurrent requests produce one order and one reservation. Takeaways Put the check and the write in one statement when you can. It's simpler than explicit locking. Order your locks to avoid deadlocks. Reserve at order time , not cart time. Design so correctness never waits on a background job . Make checkout idempotent ; mobile networks will test it for you. The full case study, with the architecture diagram, the per-domain routing and the outbox pattern, is here: ShopKit PK case study . I'm Ahmad, a full-stack React and Node.js developer. If you're building something with tricky data or e-commerce rules, let's talk .

title: Calculating EU PPWR Article 24 Empty-Space Ratios (<=50%) for E-Commerce Boxes in Pure JavaScript
summary: Under the European Union's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation ( Regulation (EU) 2025/40 , PPWR), Article 24 introduces a 50% maximum empty-space ratio for grouped, transport, and e-commerce mailer packaging—and void fillers such as air pillows, bubble wrap, and crinkle paper count as empty space , not product volume. When building custom packaging configurators or cartonization scripts for DTC brands shipping to Europe, checking internal box volume against clustered SKU geometry upfront prevents non-compliant stock box selection. 1. Bounding-Box & Flute Caliper Clearance Formula Corrugated mailers (such as E-flute ~1.6 mm or B-flute ~3.0 mm) require internal folding clearance beyond raw product dimensions, especially on double-wall roll-end tuck-top (RETT) mailers: export function evaluatePpwrVoidRatio ( productClusterMm , innerBoxMm ) { const productVolMm3 = productClusterMm . l * productClusterMm . w * productClusterMm . h ; const boxVolMm3 = innerBoxMm . l * innerBoxMm . w * innerBoxMm . h ; if ( boxVolMm3 <= 0 || boxVolMm3 < productVolMm3 ) { throw new Error ( 'Inner box dimensions must enclose the product cluster.' ) ; } const emptySpaceRatio = ( ( boxVolMm3 - productVolMm3 ) / boxVolMm3 ) * 100 ; const maxCompliantBoxVolCm3 = ( productVolMm3 / 0.5 ) / 1000 ; return { productVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( productVolMm3 / 1000 ) , innerBoxVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( boxVolMm3 / 1000 ) , emptySpacePct : Number ( emptySpaceRatio . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , compliant : emptySpaceRatio <= 50 , maxAllowedBoxVolumeCm3 : Math . round ( maxCompliantBoxVolCm3 ) } ; } 2. Why Stock Cartons Fail Multi-Item Beauty & Confectionery Kits A common failure pattern in subscription and DTC fulfillment is dropping a 180 × 120 × 65 mm skincare jar cluster ( 1,404 cm³ ) into a standard 260 × 200 × 110 mm ( 5,720 cm³ ) stock corrugated mailer stuffed with paper shreds. Even though the box feels full, its statutory empty-space ratio is 75.5% —well above the 50% threshold. Right-sizing to a 200 × 140 × 80 mm ( 2,240 cm³ ) custom E-flute mailer brings the empty-space ratio down to 37.3% while cutting dimensional freight weight. 3. title: Today in AI: a claimed 9/4 matrix multiplication result, a shorter Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, and a code golf record
summary: Three AI stories from the last 48 hours that are worth a builder's attention. 1. OpenAI claims the matrix multiplication exponent is exactly 9/4 Per Scott Aaronson's write-up, OpenAI says it proved the exponent omega equals 9/4, with the lower bound matching the known upper bound. If it holds up, it closes a question researchers have chased for decades. It still needs independent review. 2. Anthropic posts a much shorter Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Luke Sernau and colleagues cut the machine-checked proof from about 300k lines to about 76k. It is verified by software, but no mathematician has read it end to end yet. The thing to scrutinize is whether the formal definitions say what we actually mean, because Lean only checks the proof against the statement as written. 3. GPT-6.2 Astra beats the 2015 Google code golfers A new benchmark has it scoring about 92% on JS, Python and C++, ahead of the 2015 human results. Code golf rewards search and experimentation, not only recall, which is why it is a decent signal for agentic work. The comment threads also show people debating whether the model regressed on chat and writing. The pattern Models are getting spiky: superhuman where a cheap verifier exists, flatter elsewhere. That makes verification, not generation, the bottleneck. Which of these is actually changing how you work? Curious where you land.

title: My NAS disks never rested. The cause was Docker healthchecks.
summary: I run about 90 containers in 60 stacks on a Synology DS923+: four hard drives, btrfs, RAID 5. For months the drives ticked all night. Disk 1 sat at 77–88 % busy while nothing was happening, and the IO load average hovered between 5 and 8. It wasn't Jellyfin, Immich or a backup job. It was healthchecks. Why a healthcheck writes to disk Every time Docker runs a healthcheck probe, it records the result in the container's state and saves that state to disk. That's a small write plus an fsync. One container probing every 30 seconds is nothing. But many compose examples ship with 5- or 10-second intervals, and once you have forty containers with healthchecks you have a steady stream of small synchronous writes. On btrfs (copy-on-write, checksummed metadata) over RAID 5 (a partial-stripe write means read, modify, write), each of those tiny writes turns into several physical ones. The disks never get to rest. Measure your own List every container's healthcheck interval: docker ps -q | xargs docker inspect \ --format '{{.Name}} {{if .Config.Healthcheck}}{{.Config.Healthcheck.Interval}}{{else}}none{{end}}' 0s means Docker's default of 30 seconds. Add up 60 / interval for every container and you have your probes per minute. Mine was 232 . Then watch the disks for a few minutes with nothing else running: iostat -x 5 if you have it, or the disk utilisation graph in your NAS's resource monitor. The fix Give everything that doesn't need second-by-second detection a 60-second interval: healthcheck : test : [ "CMD" , "wget" , "-qO-" , "http://localhost:8080/health" ] interval : 60s timeout : 10s retries : 3 start_period : 60s start_period keeps a slow first start from counting as a failure. If your Docker Engine is version 25 or newer, start_interval: 5s lets it probe quickly during that start period only. Don't delete the healthchecks. They're what depends_on: condition: service_healthy waits for, and what tells you a container is up but not actually working. Results Moving 15 stacks from 5–10 s intervals to 60 s: Before After Healthcheck probes per minute 232 94 Write IOPS at idle ~380–440 ~295 Disk 1 busy at idle 77–88 % 57 % IO load average 5–8 2–3 It was the biggest single improvement I made to that NAS, and it took ten minutes. What else made the box calm Healthchecks were chapter one of a longer list: Redeploying one stack at a time and checking it's running and healthy before the next. A batch of 30 Portainer updates at once took down about 70 containers on this box. The DSM boot-order trap : Container Manager starts containers one by one after a restart, so an MQTT broker can come up 25 minutes late. restart: always on the few that matter fixes it. Memory caps on every container, so one leak can't take the house down. No dashboard mounts docker.sock : a read-only socket proxy answers their questions instead. I wrote all of it up as The Quiet NAS : a 44-page guide plus 26 ready-to-use files (compose stacks, scripts, a Home Assistant disk-health alert and checklists). Most of it works on any Docker host with hard drives; the Synology-only parts are marked. → The Quiet NAS Code LAUNCH25 takes 25 % off until Monday 30 November. I'm the author. Happy to answer questions in the comments, especially if your numbers look different from mine.

title: A popularity table of my skills opens with the last step
summary: He asked for a list of his agents' most popular skills, then decided the first 20 rows should be tasks, not a ranking. The fleet counter backs the decision: 277 skills on the shelf, 3,354 calls since June, the top 20 take 71% of all calls - and #1 is the end-of-session retro at 31%. A popularity table opens with the last thing you do, not the first 1. ⭐⭐⭐ The ranking he asked for, measured. Fleet skill-usage counter, _machine-bus/_metrics/skill-usage/*.jsonl , 5 writer nodes, n= 3,354 calls, 2026-06-06 → 2026-11-24, 182 distinct names. Top of the list: retro 1,050 (31.3%) · dr-fanout 150 · claudeai-sync 129 · alpha-judge 128 · tt 106 · voice-sessions 97 · alfa-search-recall-deepresearch 94 · intake 65 · intention 58 · coach 56. Top 20 = 70.7% of all calls. 2. ⭐⭐⭐ Why a popularity list fails a newcomer. Row 1 is the retrospective that closes a session. Rows 3, 4 and 6 are mostly background work: syncing old web chats, a judge for mined candidates, voice notes turned into sessions. Rows 2 and 7 are deep-research rituals. Someone arriving with "I need to answer a lead" or "my machines stopped syncing" finds neither verb in the first ten rows. The list answers "what runs most", and the question was "where do I start". 3. ⭐⭐ The long tail is almost half the shelf. On this node 277 skills have a SKILL.md . 160 were called at least once anywhere in the fleet; 117 (42%) never. 66 names were called once or twice. A table sorted by calls would bury nearly half the shelf below row 160, including runbooks that are supposed to sit at zero until the day they are needed ( runbook_skills.txt lists 27 of them, e.g. raise-sync , reboot ). 4. ⭐⭐ The ranking also splits one tool in two. systematic-debugging 41 + superpowers:systematic-debugging 40 : the same skill under two names, each landing around rows 18-19. Merged, it is 81 calls and row 9. A popularity table built straight from the counter would show it twice and rank it too low. 5. ⭐⭐ The counter itself has been half-blind since October. Last write per node: hub 2026-10-02 · ZBOOK 2026-10-02 · MacBook 2026-10-01 · anchor 2026-08-18 · this node 2026-11-24 . For the last ~55 days only one machine reports. The ranking above describes June-September work, not this month. 6. What the task-first table needs that the counter cannot give. Skill descriptions are written for the router, not for the reader: median 338 characters, 14 over the 400-character limit. A task row needs a short human verb ("answer a lead", "the sync is down", "prepare for a call") and one arrow to one skill. That mapping is editorial work - the counter can only tell which rows deserve a place in the top 20. 7. ⚠️ Limits. Counts are invocations logged by a hook, not completed work; routine-triggered calls ( origin:unknown , 40+ of them) are mixed with human ones. Shelf numbers are this node's receive-only copy. title: Teaching AI About Disordered Proteins? I’d Start at 50 Milliseconds
summary: If AlphaFold gives you 25 different pictures of two proteins bound together, which one would you trust enough to plan an experiment around? A LinkedIn post about AlphaFold and disordered proteins got me thinking about that question from the lab’s side. I think there’s a specific gap we can fill with FastHDX. We can measure which stretches of a disordered protein change when a partner binds, including changes that are visible only in the first fraction of a second of labelling. Put those measurements in a public databank and the same experiment can help one team judge a structure today and another train a model to predict which regions will respond in the next protein pair. One team really did have 25 models to choose from In a study of the progesterone receptor and its partner SRC3 , Matthew Mann and colleagues generated 25 AlphaFold 3 models. Both proteins have large disordered regions. Across predictions, one of the things that varied most was where the two proteins sat relative to each other. The researchers used hydrogen–deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) and a program called HDXer to identify the model that best fit their measurements for visualization. You can download the experimental data from PRIDE under PXD056400 . An intrinsically disordered protein (IDP), or an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) within a larger protein, can sample many shapes. Some regions settle into a fold when they bind. Others stay mobile even with a partner attached. In a benchmark of known complexes , AlphaFold-Multimer produced at least acceptable structures for more than 76% of cases in each dataset. For the group that stayed particularly flexible when bound, only about 3% of predictions reached the high-quality category. That’s a good reason to use the software and an equally good reason to ask what the protein actually did in solution. What FastHDX can capture before two samples look the same In HDX-MS, a lab exposes the protein to heavy water. Hydrogens along its backbone exchange with deuterium. After a set time, the lab slows the exchange, cuts the protein into short pieces called peptides, and measures how much deuterium each peptide picked up. Run the protein alone and again with its partner already bound. A peptide that takes up less deuterium in the complex has become more protected. The partner might touch that stretch directly, or binding elsewhere might stabilize it. The progesterone receptor study’s first labelled sample was at 10 seconds . Why would I want to start earlier? Consider a domain of CREB-binding protein. In an early experiment, exchange was nearly complete across the free domain by ten seconds . When researchers measured the same region on a millisecond timescale , they could distinguish its fast-exchanging ends from its slower centre. Adding its binding partner, ACTR, protected the centre further. A ten-second reading alone could miss what made those regions different. Nicoya specifies a labelling range of 50 milliseconds to 24 hours for FastHDX . It automates the mixing and quenching upstream of the mass spectrometer. That means I can put the free protein and the complex on the same schedule, early enough to catch fast exchange and long enough to follow the protected stretches. Here, 50 milliseconds is the time the sample spends in heavy water. The partners have already had time to bind. There’s a disordered protein example from the instrument’s own history. Neeleema Seetaloo and colleagues studied full-length, monomeric α-synuclein on the FastHDX prototype called ms2min . Across the solution conditions they tested, faster exchange around residues 115–135 correlated with a shorter wait for aggregation to begin. The sequence was identical every time. The exchange curves and the buffer tell a model something the sequence alone can’t. Where the data go, and who already uses them The developers of HDXRank collected experimental HDX data from PRIDE and MassIVE , trained a model to rank candidate structures of protein complexes, and released their training dataset . For training and evaluation, they chose 30 seconds to 10 minutes because that interval contained the most uptake measurements. That’s where I see an opening for labs with FastHDX. We can contribute paired measurements in the first second, while some of the most flexible peptides are still picking up label. What we can share Where another team can find it Raw spectra, peptide uptake tables and experimental conditions Deposit them together in PRIDE or MassIVE . For a real example, a study of engineered protein switches used ms2min from 100 milliseconds to 100 seconds and deposited its HDX data as PXD073666 . Published experimental evidence that a particular sequence region is disordered Submit the evidence to DisProt for curation. Its α-synuclein entry shows how readers can trace a regional annotation back to an experiment. A set of three-dimensional conformations built or refined using the data Deposit the ensemble in the Protein Ensemble Database and link it to the experimental dataset so researchers can examine both. What I’d actually give a model developer Suppose one peptide takes up 3.0 daltons alone and 1.8 with its partner at 250 milliseconds . By ten seconds, both samples reach 5.0. Those numbers are hypothetical. Here’s how I’d use them. Give the model the two sequences, the peptide’s position, the solution conditions and the labelling time. Ask it to predict the change in uptake. The measured answer is −1.2 daltons at 250 milliseconds and zero at ten seconds . A peptide the lab never detected gets marked as missing. That ten-second zero is worth keeping. For a pilot, I’d measure one known pair at 50 ms, 250 ms, 1 s, 10 s and 1 minute. Two states and three independent repeats make 30 timed measurements. At Nicoya’s stated 8 µL per time point , that’s 240 µL for the timed measurements , before controls and handling losses. The autosampler lets a lab queue additional pairs on that same schedule. I’d publish one row per peptide, state, time and replicate, with the raw file reference, sequences, concentrations, pH, temperature and deuterium fraction, following the HDX-MS reporting recommendations . Once enough families are represented, I’d hold one entire protein family back from training. Give two models the same measurement budget, let one learn from early and late data and the other from later times alone, then ask each to rank the held-out peptides by how much binding protects them. The useful result for a lab is whether those first few time points change which stretch it would investigate next. That’s why I’d choose FastHDX to help build this dataset. We can always take another model back to an archived spectrum. We can’t take a ten-second sample back to 250 milliseconds to recover a difference that’s already gone. If we want AI to get better at disordered proteins, I’d start by making those first 50 milliseconds as easy to download as a predicted structure. title: C# 15 Unpacked: Popping the Hood on Labeled Loops and Finding No Labels at All
summary: All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself. georgekobaidze / dotnet11-playground A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15. .NET 11 & C# 15 Playground A lightweight playground repository for experimenting with and testing new features introduced in .NET 11 and C# 15 . Use it to explore language changes, try out APIs, and validate ideas in isolation without production constraints. Each feature lives in its own small project, often with a "before" and "after" version so you can see what the new feature actually changes. What's inside Project Feature Description Unions Union types Console examples: the login flow (before and after unions), plus samples for parsing input, a state machine, user commands, and combining types you don't own. UnionsWebApi Union types A minimal API that returns a union from a service and maps each outcome to an HTTP response. More examples will be added as new features are explored. Getting started You'll need the .NET 11 SDK . Then clone the repo and run any example: dotnet run … View on GitHub Follow me on GitHub for more updates! Table of Contents Where We Left Off Time to Pop the Hood The Decompiler Has Its Own Ideas Decoding the Trick Bonus: Two Compiler Tricks Hiding in Plain Sight So What Does This Mean? Wrapping Up Where We Left Off In my previous article , we looked at labeled break and continue , the retro new feature in C# 15 that Java has had since 1996. We used it to skip an entire order the moment we found an out-of-stock item: nextOrder : foreach ( string [ ] order in orders ) { Console . WriteLine ( "New order:" ) ; foreach ( string item in order ) { if ( item == "OUT_OF_STOCK" ) { Console . WriteLine ( " Item missing, skipping this order." ) ; continue nextOrder ; // jump to the next ORDER, not the next item } Console . WriteLine ( $ " Packing {item}" ) ; } Console . WriteLine ( " Order shipped!" ) ; } Clean, readable, and no bool flags. Time to Pop the Hood Every new C# feature is a promise from the compiler: "write it this way, and I'll take care of the rest." And every time, I want to see what "the rest" actually looks like. Here's a quick refresher on what happens to your C# code: The C# compiler turns your code into IL (Intermediate Language) and stores it in a DLL. At runtime, the JIT compiler turns that IL into machine code for your CPU, and that's what actually runs. The direction is always one way: C# → IL → machine code. Your original C# source never ends up in the DLL. That's where labels get interesting. IL has no labels, no loops, no break , and no continue . It only has branch instructions that jump to offsets. So by the time your code is compiled, the labels are gone. So how can a tool like ILSpy show us C# at all? It doesn't have our source code. It reads the DLL and rebuilds C# from what's inside: The metadata tells it the names of types, methods, and their signatures, so those come back exactly right. The IL tells it what each method does, as a flat list of instructions and jumps. ILSpy has to figure out which loops, if s, and break s would produce those jumps. Some things can't be recovered at all. Local variable names, for example, aren't stored in the IL, so ILSpy invents its own. In other words, decompiled C# isn't your code. It's a reconstruction: C# that compiles to equivalent IL. And that raises a fun question: if the labels are gone, what does ILSpy rebuild when we hand it our labeled loop? The Decompiler Has Its Own Ideas The answer turned out to be more interesting than I expected. ILSpy didn't give me back my original code. It restructured the inner loop into something I never wrote, and it's a pretty clever trick. I built the project in Release mode, opened the DLL in ILSpy, and asked it to decompile the Program class back into C#. Here's what came out: Same behavior, but a completely different shape. My nextOrder: label is gone. My inner foreach is gone. And my continue nextOrder; turned into a plain, unlabeled break . Decoding the Trick At first glance, this looks wrong. Where did the continue nextOrder; go? And why is "Order shipped!" now inside a loop? Here's what ILSpy did: My code ILSpy's version Inner foreach (string item in order) A while (true) loop with a manual index ( num ) and a bounds check continue nextOrder; break; out of the while (true) Moving to the next item num++; followed by continue; Inner loop finishing normally The bounds check fails, then "Order shipped!", then break; The key is what comes after the while (true) loop: nothing. The outer foreach body ends right there. So breaking out of the inner loop drops you straight into the next iteration of the outer loop, which is exactly what continue nextOrder; did. The "Order shipped!" line moved inside the loop so it only runs on the "all items packed" path. The out-of-stock path breaks out before reaching it. ILSpy took a labeled jump across two loops and turned it into a plain break out of a single loop. It's clever, and it's definitely not code a human would write. Bonus: Two Compiler Tricks Hiding in Plain Sight While we're here, the decompiled code reveals two things the C# compiler does with every foreach over an array, labeled or not: There's no enumerator. A foreach over an array doesn't call GetEnumerator() . The compiler turns it into a plain index-based loop, because that's faster. That's where num and array3.Length come from. Hidden temporary variables. array2 = array and array3 = obj are extra locals the compiler introduces for foreach over arrays. They copy the reference, not the array itself. You never wrote them, but they're part of how the loop is lowered. None of this is new in C# 15, but it's a nice reminder of how much the compiler rewrites behind the scenes, even for the simplest loops. So What Does This Mean? Let's put it all together. The label is a compile-time thing only. nextOrder: helps you say which loop you mean, and it helps the compiler check that you're only jumping to a loop you're actually inside. Once the compiler has done that check, the label has nothing left to do, so it doesn't make it into the IL at all. There's no runtime cost. The entire continue nextOrder; becomes a single jump instruction. The old bool flag approach would need an extra local variable, an assignment, and an extra check after the inner loop. The labeled version needs one jump, and the JIT just sees a branch like any other. And at the IL level, everything is a jump. In the previous article, I asked whether labeled loops are just goto in a nicer suit. After popping the hood, the honest answer is that in IL, everything is goto . Your for loops, your while loops, your if statements, your break and continue : they all end up as br , brtrue , brfalse , and blt . The difference between goto and a labeled continue isn't in the IL. It's in what the compiler lets you do before it gets there. goto lets you jump almost anywhere. A labeled continue only lets you jump to the next iteration of a loop you're inside. Same instruction at the end, very different rules on the way in. Wrapping Up Here's what we found under the hood: The decompiled C# doesn't look like the original. ILSpy rebuilt our inner loop as a while (true) and turned continue nextOrder; into a plain break , because decompiled code is a reconstruction, not our source. continue nextOrder; compiles to a single jump instruction. IL has no loops or labels, only branches, so the whole feature boils down to one jump to the right place. Labels don't exist at runtime. They're a compile-time tool for readability and safety, with zero runtime cost. So, the feature named after labels doesn't have a single label left after compilation. Kind of poetic, isn't it? All the code from this article is in my .NET 11 playground: dotnet11-playground . Clone it, open it in ILSpy, and see for yourself. Have you ever opened your own code in a decompiler and barely recognized it? Tell me about it in the comments. 👇 Let's stay connected! 💼 Connect with me on LinkedIn 💻 Explore my projects on GitHub 📱 Follow me on X 🎥 Watch my videos on YouTube 💬 Let's Chat on Discord

title: How vibedom turns a website's look into a procedural soundscape
summary: Paste a URL into vibedom and it plays a soundtrack built from that site's design. A scraper reads the page, a JSON "Sound Seed" is produced, and Tone.js synthesises pad, drone and arpeggio in the browser: no samples, no account, no audio file to download. I built it as a CS student at the University of Málaga. The code is open source ( germantes/vibedom , MIT). From URL to seed A scan is POST /api/scan . The server first checks the URL, including a DNS lookup, so the scraper cannot be pointed at private or reserved addresses. Every redirect and stylesheet goes through the same guard. The scraper then fetches the HTML and up to four stylesheets with plain fetch . There is no headless browser, so it does not see computed CSS or JavaScript-rendered markup. Each fetch has an 8-second timeout, the whole scrape a 20-second budget, and bodies are capped at 2 MB. The User-Agent is VibeDomBot/1.0 ; a 403, 429 or 5xx is retried once with a browser-like header. What it keeps is a compact aesthetic fingerprint: Semantics: <title> , meta description or og:description , up to five <h1> s, and a short text sample. Colour: hex and rgb() values from the CSS, plus meta theme-color . Background comes from html / body / :root when those rules exist; otherwise the most frequent CSS colour. Relative luminance decides isDark (threshold 0.4). Type: font-family declarations, grouped into serif , sans-serif , monospace or display . Motion: whether the CSS contains animation / @keyframes or transition . The HTML of the scanned site is not stored. The public ranking keeps only the domain and the UTC day of the scan, never the path, query string or IP. Those signals become a Sound Seed, from Gemini on Vertex AI or from a local composer, then pass through normalizeSeed() : invalid types and enums fail, out-of-range numbers are clipped, free text is truncated. Successful AI seeds for the same URL stay in an in-memory cache for six hours (up to 500 entries). The cache dies when the process restarts. If you do not want to send a URL, the landing still plays three static presets (Cyberpunk, Editorial, Indie pastel). The Sound Seed The seed is the contract between analysis and playback. This is the real Stripe seed from the Sound tests page: { "metadata" : { "url" : "https://stripe.com/" , "detectedVibe" : "Sleek, high-tech financial infrastructure" , "explanation" : "The clean, bright background combined with vibrant violet accents and dynamic animations translates to a fast-paced, highly structured lydian soundscape with crisp arpeggios that open up as you scroll." } , "uiTheme" : { "backgroundColor" : "#ffffff" , "accentColor" : "#533afd" , "textColor" : "#161741" , "fontFamily" : "sans-serif" } , "musicalParams" : { "bpm" : 92 , "rootNote" : "G" , "scale" : "lydian" , "octave" : 4 } , "synthConfig" : { "pad" : { "waveform" : "triangle" , "attack" : 1.5 , "release" : 3 , "filterFreq" : 2500 } , "arp" : { "enabled" : true , "waveform" : "sine" , "density" : 0.65 , "delayWet" : 0.4 } , "effects" : { "reverbDecay" : 4.5 , "reverbWet" : 0.3 , "chorusDepth" : 0.25 } , "interactivity" : { "scrollTarget" : "filterFreq" , "scrollMultiplier" : 2.5 , "hoverNoteTrigger" : true } } } uiTheme is applied to the landing so the page visually becomes the site you pasted. Scales are major , minor , dorian , phrygian , lydian or pentatonic ; waveforms are sine , triangle , sawtooth or square . Tempo sits between 40 and 140 BPM. The playground exposes the same JSON and live sliders. The model, and the composer that does not need one The translator is a short "synesthetic music director" prompt plus structured output from a Gemini model served through Vertex AI. The schema is the seed itself, so the model has to fill metadata , uiTheme , musicalParams and synthConfig . The prompt uses the same rules as the local composer: a dark background leans toward minor, phrygian or dorian, a slower tempo and a closed filter; a light one toward major or lydian and a more open filter; saturated colours get more chorus and saw/square waves; serif type gets longer reverb; animations raise tempo and arpeggio density. detectedVibe and explanation follow the language of the vibedom page (Spanish or English), not of the scanned site. Technical field names stay in English. In production the backend talks to Vertex AI (Google Cloud) with a service account; the plain Gemini API with GEMINI_KEY is only kept as a fallback for local development. The default model list is gemini-3.5-flash , then gemini-3.5-flash-lite , then gemini-3.6-flash . Each call has a 20-second attempt timeout and a 30-second overall deadline, with exponential backoff and jitter. If one model fails, the next is tried. Thinking is set to "low" because the schema already constrains the answer. When the key is missing, the quota is spent, or the call errors, the scan does not go silent. composeLocalSeed() applies the same rules with plain arithmetic: luminance, accent saturation, font category and motion flags decide BPM, scale, waveforms, filter, reverb and whether the arpeggio is on. A short FNV-1a hash of a stable fingerprint (final URL, title, colours, font, motion) picks the remaining variations, so the same site with the same signals always yields the same seed. The UI language never changes the music, only the visible copy. The seed is marked metadata.source: "local" , and the landing says so. If a site blocks automated reads, a variation can still be derived from the URL alone, and the copy says the palette could not be read. Playing the seed createSoundscape() builds a small graph, tuned for modest CPUs: a sine drone; a pad ( PolySynth with a fat* oscillator, two detuned voices) through a low-pass filter; and an arpeggio ( Synth ) through its own filter and a feedback delay. Those buses meet at a chorus, then a Freeverb (cheaper than a convolution reverb), a limiter and the master output. An analyser and an FFT feed the visualisers. The master fades in over 2.5 seconds. Tone.js is injected, not bundled, and loads only after the first click. Harmony is generated, not read from a file. Chord degrees follow a Markov-style walk that favours fourths and fifths, soft third motions and a pull back to the tonic, and never repeats the current degree. Diminished fifths are skipped. Each new pad voicing is octave-transposed toward the centre of the previous one so the part does not leap. The arpeggio is a short random walk on the scale, weighted toward the current chord; density is a probability per eighth-note. Scroll velocity, smoothed and decayed, modulates one parameter ( filterFreq , reverbWet , delayWet or arpDensity ). Hovering a link or button can trigger a quiet scale tone, with a short debounce. Stripe's seed above opens the filter as you scroll. None of this audio is streamed or pre-recorded. A widget under 5 KB, and no API calls The embed is a single script tag: <script src = "https://vibedom.dev/widget.js" data-seed = "<base64>" defer ></script> widget.js is under 5 KB. It decodes data-seed (the Sound Seed as UTF-8, then Base64), mounts a floating button in an open Shadow DOM with all: initial so it does not inherit or leak host CSS. The seed never leaves the snippet. There is no call to the model. On load, the widget sends one cookie-free ping with just the embedding domain (skipped under Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control), so I can see where it's used. No cookies, no localStorage , no IP stored. Labels follow <html lang> . Only the first click imports widget-player.js , which loads Tone.js from jsDelivr and starts the same engine, still inside the user gesture so the browser allows audio. Visitors hear the variation you baked in. See the install guide . Privacy choices This is a product decision, not an afterthought. vibedom has no accounts, no first-party cookies, no pixels and no third-party analytics. Music is synthesised locally. Shared long links carry the seed in the URL itself. If you copy the short link, the seed is stored for 30 days in Redis so the preview card can be served, then it expires. I would rather lose some marketing numbers than put a tracking script on a site that claims it does not profile you. What's next A few things I'm thinking about. Nothing is promised, and I'd love to hear which one you'd actually use: A browser extension , so any tab can play its own soundscape without copying the URL into vibedom. Audio export , to download a loop as WAV and use it in a video or a project. Real instruments beyond synthesizers. Tone.js already ships Tone.Sampler , so the idea is to let the seed pick an instrumentation (piano and strings for an editorial site, marimba or kalimba for a pastel one) using freely licensed sample banks, loaded only when you press play so the widget stays tiny. If you have ideas, or a site you want to hear, leave a comment. Try it English landing: vibedom.dev/en Ten real sound tests (Stripe, Apple, Wikipedia, Nike and others): vibedom.dev/en/sound-tests Playground with the raw seed: vibedom.dev/playground/en Source: github.com/germantes/vibedom If you try it on your own site, I am curious which mapping surprised you: the scale, the filter, or the way the scroll opens the sound.

title: Build a Time-Zone-Safe Itinerary Validator in Python
summary: A travel itinerary looks like a sequence of cards: a museum at 10:00, lunch at 12:30, and a train later in the day. Underneath those cards, however, is a scheduling problem. Time zones, daylight-saving transitions, inconsistent supplier data, and missing transfer time can make a plan impossible even when every individual booking is valid. This tutorial builds a small, dependency-free itinerary validator in Python. It will not invent journey durations or decide whether a restaurant is open. Instead, it will check the facts a travel application already has, report conflicts, and explain why a proposed schedule needs attention. Store instants, not just clock labels Imagine an itinerary containing these two values: Flight arrival: 14:10 Hotel check-in: 14:45 The 35-minute gap seems clear until you ask which time zone each value uses. The labels might refer to different cities, or a supplier might have stripped the UTC offset. A scheduling engine should not guess. Require an ISO 8601 timestamp that includes an explicit offset, such as 2027-04-07T10:00:00+02:00. This identifies a real instant. Keep the IANA time-zone name (Europe/Paris, for example) as separate metadata for display and future date calculations. An offset and a time zone are not interchangeable. Paris is not always UTC+02:00. Its offset changes seasonally. For recurring events or future local-time creation, a time-zone database is essential. Define a minimal event contract Our prototype uses three event fields and two planning fields: start and end: offset-aware timestamps label: a human-readable activity name travel_after_min: the estimated transfer time required after this event zone: the IANA time zone used by the activity's local clock The transfer estimate must come from a routing provider, a tour operator, or a clearly labeled user assumption. A validator should never quietly substitute a made-up travel duration. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime, timezone from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo @dataclass(frozen=True) class Event: label: str start: str end: str zone: str travel_after_min: int = 0 def parse_instant(value: str, zone: str) -> datetime: dt = datetime.fromisoformat(value) if dt.tzinfo is None or dt.utcoffset() is None: raise ValueError(f"Missing UTC offset: {value}") # Reject an offset that disagrees with the named local time zone. local = dt.astimezone(ZoneInfo(zone)) if local.replace(tzinfo=None) != dt.replace(tzinfo=None): raise ValueError(f"Local time/zone mismatch: {value} / {zone}") if local.utcoffset() != dt.utcoffset(): raise ValueError(f"UTC offset/zone mismatch: {value} / {zone}") return dt.astimezone(timezone.utc) A useful property of this contract is that both the original local time and the absolute instant survive. It also catches one common data error: a summer timestamp labeled with an impossible winter offset for its city. The zoneinfo module uses an IANA time-zone database available to the Python runtime; some environments require installing system time-zone data or the tzdata package. Check durations, overlaps, and transfer buffers An event can be valid in isolation while making the overall plan impossible. Two 90-minute attractions may overlap; a transfer could require 30 minutes while the itinerary provides only 15. def validate_itinerary(events: list[Event]) -> list[str]: issues = [] normalized = [] for event in events: start = parse_instant(event.start, event.zone) end = parse_instant(event.end, event.zone) if end <= start: issues.append(f"{event.label}: end must be after start") if event.travel_after_min < 0: issues.append(f"{event.label}: negative transfer estimate") normalized.append((start, end, event)) Sorting by UTC avoids incorrect comparisons across time zones. normalized.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) for previous, current in zip(normalized, normalized[1:]): _, previous_end, old = previous current_start, _, new = current gap_min = (current_start - previous_end).total_seconds() / 60 if gap_min < 0: issues.append( f"{old.label} overlaps {new.label} by {-gap_min:g} min" ) elif gap_min < old.travel_after_min: issues.append( f"{old.label} -> {new.label}: {gap_min:g} min available; " f"{old.travel_after_min} min transfer required" ) return issues This approach is intentionally strict: a missing UTC offset raises an error instead of producing a plausible-looking but untrustworthy result. For a production API, convert that exception into a structured validation response that identifies the affected record. Notice another design choice: the transfer requirement belongs to the preceding event. That is not the only possible data model. A richer route graph would attach transfer estimates to each pair of locations and travel mode, and might represent transfers as their own scheduled events. Our simpler model is sufficient to demonstrate the principle. Run a small example These example appointments are deliberately fictional; they are not live opening hours, reservations, or walking-time estimates. plan = [ Event( label="Museum visit", start="2027-04-07T10:00:00+02:00", end="2027-04-07T11:30:00+02:00", zone="Europe/Paris", travel_after_min=45, ), Event( label="Lunch", start="2027-04-07T12:30:00+02:00", end="2027-04-07T13:30:00+02:00", zone="Europe/Paris", travel_after_min=20, ), Event( label="Afternoon walk", start="2027-04-07T13:45:00+02:00", end="2027-04-07T14:30:00+02:00", zone="Europe/Paris", ), ] for issue in validate_itinerary(plan): print(issue) The first interval provides 60 minutes for a 45-minute transfer, so it passes. The second provides 15 minutes for a transfer estimated at 20 minutes, so the script reports: Lunch -> Afternoon walk: 15 min available; 20 min transfer required This is an explanation, not a mysterious red warning icon. It tells a traveler or trip planner which assumption has failed. Prove the validator catches time-zone mistakes Unit tests are more valuable than screenshots of a calendar. Start with two focused checks: an impossible offset and a missing transfer buffer. def test_mismatched_paris_offset(): try: parse_instant("2027-07-10T09:00:00+01:00", "Europe/Paris") except ValueError: pass else: raise AssertionError("Expected a time-zone mismatch") def test_transfer_conflict(): result = validate_itinerary(plan) assert len(result) == 1 assert "15 min available" in result[0] test_mismatched_paris_offset() test_transfer_conflict() For production, also test overnight activities, invalid IANA zones, clock changes, duplicate reservations, canceled events, and departure/arrival records across different countries. During a daylight-saving fall-back, the same wall-clock time can occur twice. Requiring a timestamp with an explicit offset helps disambiguate the instant, but you should still test it against the named zone. Separate validation from optimization A validator answers: Is this itinerary internally consistent under the supplied assumptions? An optimizer answers: Can we find a better itinerary? Those are different responsibilities. A robust architecture can use a pipeline: Ingest: collect opening hours, reservations, transit details, and user preferences from their original sources. Normalize: preserve source identifiers, local times, offsets, zone names, and update timestamps. Validate: reject malformed events and flag impossible transfers or overlaps. Optimize: suggest alternative ordering or times only after validation succeeds. Present: distinguish verified facts from estimates and clearly label unresolved conflicts. If a provider changes a departure time, the itinerary should be revalidated before new recommendations appear. Never silently convert a 45-minute transfer estimate into a 10-minute one just to make the schedule fit. A practical data provenance checklist Travel products often combine supplier feeds, map routing, editorial destination guides, and user-created notes. Treating all four as equally authoritative is a recipe for misleading plans. A small provenance record can prevent this: { "field": "travel_after_min", "value": 45, "source_type": "user_estimate", "verified": false, "recorded_at": "2026-11-26T14:00:00Z" } In a live service, this metadata lets the interface say "45-minute transfer, estimated by traveler" rather than displaying the duration as a confirmed routing calculation. The same pattern is useful for attraction hours and seasonal restrictions. If information is stale, make that visible before a customer purchases a ticket. For Persian-language destination context and the broader travel-and-tourism ecosystem, Gashtanio publishes related material for readers exploring places and travel choices. The engineering principle remains universal: reliable itineraries should make their assumptions inspectable. What to build next This sample is deliberately not a route planner. It does not geocode locations, calculate road or rail journey times, check tickets, or query real-time availability. Those should arrive through dedicated services with explicit provenance and error handling. A useful next iteration would introduce an itinerary_version, store the validation result with its data-source revisions, and rerun checks whenever a supplier changes a reservation. Another extension would distinguish hard constraints (a booked flight) from soft preferences (a preferred lunch time). The goal is not to build a perfect vacation app in one Python file. It is to make a very common class of scheduling error measurable and explainable before it reaches a traveler. Disclosure: This educational article was drafted with AI assistance. The examples use fictional itinerary data and should be tested against real requirements before production deployment. Gashtanio is an affiliated publication mentioned for contextual reading.

title: Design a Trustworthy Vehicle Maintenance Timeline in Python
summary: A car-history app looks simple until two data sources disagree. One workshop reports a brake service at 62,000 kilometers. An inspection center records 61,500 kilometers a week later. Another provider sends the same service record twice, using slightly different timestamps. If the application merely sorts those rows by date, the result may look convincing while quietly misleading the reader. The hard part is not drawing the timeline. It is designing a trustworthy event pipeline behind it. In this tutorial, we'll build a small Python prototype for receiving vehicle maintenance events, normalizing them, detecting duplicates, and surfacing inconsistencies without pretending that the software knows which source is correct. Start with events, not a single vehicle record A typical early design stores one mutable object per vehicle: { "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "last_service": "2026-10-02", "odometer_km": 62000 } This is convenient for a dashboard, but it loses the questions that matter: Who provided the reading? When did the service actually happen? When did the system receive it? Was an earlier reading overwritten? Instead, represent each observation as an event. A derived vehicle summary can still exist, but the source events remain available for inspection. { "event_id": "workshop-A:invoice-781", "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "event_type": "service", "occurred_at": "2026-10-02T09:30:00+03:30", "received_at": "2026-10-03T08:15:00Z", "odometer_km": 62000, "source": "workshop-A" } The two timestamps serve different purposes. occurred_at describes the claimed real-world event. received_at describes when the application learned about it. Keeping both makes delayed imports and backdated corrections easier to investigate. Define a small, explicit validation boundary The following code uses only Python's standard library. It intentionally handles a narrow event schema rather than trying to anticipate every workshop, insurer, or inspection system. from datetime import datetime, timezone ALLOWED_TYPES = {"service", "inspection", "repair", "odometer"} def to_utc(value: str) -> datetime: parsed = datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00")) if parsed.tzinfo is None: raise ValueError("Timestamp must include a UTC offset") return parsed.astimezone(timezone.utc) def normalize_event(raw: dict) -> dict: required = { "event_id", "vehicle_id", "event_type", "occurred_at", "received_at", "odometer_km", "source" } missing = required - raw.keys() if missing: raise ValueError(f"Missing fields: {sorted(missing)}") if raw["event_type"] not in ALLOWED_TYPES: raise ValueError("Unknown event type") if not all(isinstance(raw[key], str) and raw[key].strip() for key in ("event_id", "vehicle_id", "source")): raise ValueError("Identifiers and source must be nonempty strings") reading = raw["odometer_km"] if reading is not None and (type(reading) is not int or reading < 0): raise ValueError("odometer_km must be a nonnegative integer or null") return { "event_id": raw["event_id"], "vehicle_id": raw["vehicle_id"], "event_type": raw["event_type"], "occurred_at": to_utc(raw["occurred_at"]), "received_at": to_utc(raw["received_at"]), "odometer_km": reading, "source": raw["source"], } Requiring an explicit time-zone offset avoids treating a local wall-clock time as if it were already UTC. Requiring an integer odometer reading also prevents ambiguous text such as "about 62k" from entering calculations unnoticed. That original text may still be useful, but it belongs in a separate raw-data record. For a production system, schema evolution, access controls, a durable event store, and country-specific vehicle identifiers would need separate decisions. Make repeated deliveries safe Imports are retried. Webhooks are delivered more than once. A user can upload the same file twice. These are ordinary operational events, not exceptional failures. An event_id should therefore identify a source event consistently. A database can enforce uniqueness on a combination such as (source, event_id). In a small prototype, we can illustrate the rule with a set: seen = set() accepted = [] def receive(raw: dict) -> str: event = normalize_event(raw) key = (event["source"], event["event_id"]) if key in seen: return "duplicate" seen.add(key) accepted.append(event) return "accepted" The uniqueness check and insertion must be atomic in a real database. Otherwise, two workers could simultaneously accept the same event. A repeated identifier with changed content also deserves investigation rather than a silent overwrite; retain the raw payload or a content fingerprint for comparison. Flag impossible-looking sequences without rewriting history Suppose the sorted readings for one vehicle are 48,000 km, 62,000 km, and then 61,500 km. A consumer-facing interface should not silently replace the last number with 62,000. Nor should it automatically label the lower reading fraudulent. A transcription error, replaced instrument cluster, or source-matching mistake may explain it. The safer behavior is to create a review flag: def odometer_flags(events: list[dict]) -> list[dict]: readings = sorted( (e for e in events if e["odometer_km"] is not None), key=lambda e: (e["occurred_at"], e["event_id"]), ) flags = [] for previous, current in zip(readings, readings[1:]): if current["odometer_km"] < previous["odometer_km"]: flags.append({ "type": "reading_decreased", "previous_event": previous["event_id"], "current_event": current["event_id"], }) return flags This is a consistency check, not a fraud detector. For a multi-source feed, two readings may even describe different points within the same day, with uncertain event times. A production pipeline should preserve that uncertainty instead of manufacturing precision. Other useful flags include unusually large jumps over short periods, a received timestamp far earlier than the claimed occurrence, repeated invoices with different identifiers, and mismatched vehicle identifiers. Each flag needs a documented interpretation and an escalation path. Keep provenance visible in the API An API returning only a polished timeline hides the very information readers might need to assess it. Consider returning the event and its context together: { "vehicle_id": "demo-42", "events": [ { "event_id": "workshop-A:invoice-781", "event_type": "service", "odometer_km": 62000, "source": "workshop-A", "status": "reported" } ], "review_flags": ["reading_decreased"] } A status such as reported means the application received a claim. It does not mean the claim was independently verified. If verification is performed, record who verified it, by which process, and when. Do not collapse these states into an unexplained green checkmark. For broader Persian-language discussion of vehicles, automotive technology, and the car ecosystem, Automadar provides an automotive-focused publication. The engineering lesson here is narrower: a maintenance timeline earns trust by showing where its records came from. Privacy is part of the data model Vehicle history can reveal more than a repair. Timestamps and workshop locations may expose movement patterns; owner contact details may be included in imported documents. Decide what the timeline actually needs before ingesting entire invoices. Separate identifiers used for matching from personally identifiable information. Avoid displaying raw workshop notes to other users. Define retention and correction workflows, and require authorization before exposing detailed vehicle records. If the application supports users in multiple jurisdictions, review the relevant privacy and consumer-disclosure requirements rather than assuming a single policy fits every market. Test the failure modes, not just the happy path Before releasing even a prototype, verify these cases: The same (source, event_id) arrives twice. Two sources reuse the same event ID for unrelated events. A timestamp has no time-zone offset. odometer_km is negative, a string, or a Boolean value. A late-arriving event belongs chronologically between two existing events. A corrected reading conflicts with a previously published summary. A vehicle identifier is missing or maps to more than one record. Tests should assert not only that bad data is rejected or flagged but also that no valid historical event is silently lost. The larger design lesson A vehicle-history interface is a projection of an evidence trail. Good dashboards are useful, but they cannot restore provenance that was discarded upstream. Capture claims as immutable events, keep arrival time separate from occurrence time, prevent accidental duplication, and present anomalies as reviewable facts rather than automatic verdicts. The result is a modest system that is easier to audit, correct, and extend—exactly the properties a real automotive data product needs. Disclosure: This tutorial was prepared with AI assistance. Its prototype code illustrates data-validation principles and is not a production-ready vehicle-history system.
