title: Paystack + Next.js: Payments You Can Actually Trust
summary: --- title: "Paystack + Next.js: Payments You Can Actually Trust" published: false date: 2026-11-26 08:00:00 UTC tags: Paystack,Nextjs,Payments,Security canonical_url: https://oyeleke.com.ng/blog/paystack-nextjs-integration Getting a Paystack checkout to open takes ten minutes. Getting it to be correct — every successful payment fulfilled exactly once, no fake confirmations, no orders stuck on "pending" because someone closed the tab — takes a bit more thought. This is the pattern I use for Paystack in Next.js App Router projects, including online giving on the NWPM church platform . It has four parts: Initialize the transaction on the server, with a price the server decides. Complete it on Paystack's checkout. Verify it on the server before delivering anything. Listen for webhooks, so payments are fulfilled even when the browser never comes back. The one rule The browser can start a payment. Only your server, talking to Paystack, can decide that a payment happened . Everything below follows from that. Never trust an amount the browser sends you, and never treat "the user landed on my success page" as proof of payment. Paystack's own docs say the same: visiting the callback URL doesn't prove the transaction succeeded. Setup Get your secret key from the Paystack dashboard ( Settings → API Keys & Webhooks ) and generate a webhook signing secret under Developers → API configuration . Use test keys locally. # .env.local PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY = sk_test_xxx # server only, never NEXT_PUBLIC_ PAYSTACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET = whsec_xxx # webhook signing secret NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL = http : //localhost:3000 1. A tiny server-only Paystack client // lib/paystack.ts import "server-only" ; const API = "https://api.paystack.co" ; async function paystack < T > ( path : string , init ?: RequestInit ) : Promise < T > { const res = await fetch ( `${API}${path}` , { . . . init , headers : { Authorization : `Bearer ${process.env.PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY}` , "Content-Type" : "application/json" , . . . init ? . headers , } , cache : "no-store" , } ) ; const body = await res . json ( ) ; if ( ! res . ok || ! body . status ) throw new Error ( body . message ?? `Paystack error ${res.status}` ) ; return body . data as T ; } export function initializeTransaction ( input : { email : string ; amount : number ; // in kobo (the currency's subunit) reference : string ; callback_url : string ; metadata ?: Record < string , unknown > ; } ) { return paystack < { authorization_url : string ; access_code : string ; reference : string } > ( "/transaction/initialize" , { method : "POST" , body : JSON . stringify ( input ) } , ) ; } export function verifyTransaction ( reference : string ) { return paystack < { status : string ; amount : number ; currency : string ; reference : string } > ( `/transaction/verify/${encodeURIComponent(reference)}` , ) ; } The server-only import makes the build fail if this file is ever pulled into a client component, which is exactly what you want for anything holding your secret key. 2. Initialize on the server, with your price The client sends what it wants to buy. The server decides how much it costs, creates a pending order, and asks Paystack for a checkout URL. // app/api/checkout/route.ts import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto" ; import { initializeTransaction } from "@/lib/paystack" ; import { db } from "@/lib/db" ; // your database client export async function POST ( req : Request ) { const { productId , email } = await req . json ( ) ; const product = await db . product . findUnique ( { where : { id : productId } } ) ; if ( ! product ) return Response . json ( { error : "Unknown product" } , { status : 400 } ) ; const reference = randomUUID ( ) ; await db . order . create ( { data : { reference , productId , email , amountKobo : product . priceKobo , currency : "NGN" , status : "pending" } , } ) ; const { authorization_url } = await initializeTransaction ( { email , amount : product . priceKobo , // ₦5,000 → 500000 reference , callback_url : `${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL}/checkout/complete` , metadata : { productId } , } ) ; return Response . json ( { url : authorization_url } ) ; } Two details that matter: Amounts are in the subunit. ₦5,000 is 500000 kobo. Store prices in kobo as integers everywhere and you'll never fight floating-point rounding. You own the reference. Generate it yourself and save it before calling Paystack. That reference is how every later step — verification, webhooks, retries — finds the order. 3. Send the customer to Paystack's checkout The simplest flow that works everywhere, including flaky mobile browsers, is a redirect. Return the authorization_url from your route and send the customer there. When they finish, Paystack redirects them to your callback_url with the transaction reference in the query string. The route in step 2 already returns that URL. The button just follows it: // components/PayButton.tsx "use client" ; import { useState } from "react" ; export function PayButton ( { productId , email } : { productId : string ; email : string } ) { const [ loading , setLoading ] = useState ( false ) ; async function pay ( ) { setLoading ( true ) ; const res = await fetch ( "/api/checkout" , { method : "POST" , headers : { "Content-Type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( { productId , email } ) , } ) ; if ( ! res . ok ) return setLoading ( false ) ; const { url } = await res . json ( ) ; window . location . assign ( url ) ; } return ( < button onClick = { pay } disabled = { loading } > { loading ? "Opening checkout…" : "Pay with Paystack" } </ button > ) ; } Prefer an in-page popup? Return the access_code instead and open it with Paystack's InlineJS library ( npm i @paystack/inline-js ): new Paystack().resumeTransaction(accessCode) . The server-side parts below stay exactly the same. Whichever you choose, the browser finishing checkout only means "the customer says they paid". It doesn't mark anything as paid. 4. Fulfil once, from anywhere Both the completion page and the webhook will call the same function. It verifies with Paystack, checks the amount and currency against your order, and flips the order from pending to paid exactly once. // lib/orders.ts import "server-only" ; import { db } from "@/lib/db" ; import { verifyTransaction } from "@/lib/paystack" ; export async function fulfilOrder ( reference : string ) { const order = await db . order . findUnique ( { where : { reference } } ) ; if ( ! order ) return null ; if ( order . status === "paid" ) return order ; // already done const tx = await verifyTransaction ( reference ) ; const valid = tx . status === "success" && tx . amount === order . amountKobo && tx . currency === order . currency ; if ( ! valid ) return order ; // Conditional update: only one caller can win the pending → paid transition. const { count } = await db . order . updateMany ( { where : { reference , status : "pending" } , data : { status : "paid" , paidAt : new Date ( ) } , } ) ; if ( count === 1 ) { await sendReceipt ( order ) ; // deliver value exactly once } return { . . . order , status : "paid" as const } ; } Why so careful? Check the amount. Paystack explicitly recommends it: if the amount doesn't match what you're delivering, don't deliver. Make it idempotent. The callback page and the webhook will often arrive at nearly the same moment, and Paystack retries webhooks and lets you resend events. Without the conditional pending → paid update, you'll send two receipts or ship two orders. The completion page just calls it: // app/checkout/complete/page.tsx import { fulfilOrder } from "@/lib/orders" ; export default async function CheckoutComplete ( { searchParams , } : { searchParams : Promise < { reference ?: string ; trxref ?: string } > ; } ) { const { reference , trxref } = await searchParams ; const order = await fulfilOrder ( reference ?? trxref ?? "" ) ; if ( order ? . status === "paid" ) return < h1 > Payment received — thank you !</ h1 > ; return < h1 > We & apos ; re confirming your payment . You & apos ; ll get an email shortly . </ h1 > ; } The "still confirming" state isn't a failure. If verification hasn't settled yet, the webhook will finish the job. 5. Webhooks: the part most integrations skip Users close tabs, lose network on the bus, or their phone dies right after paying. The callback page never loads — but Paystack still sends a charge.success event to your webhook URL. This is what makes your integration reliable. Paystack now signs events with a Paystack-Signature header, using a webhook signing secret ( whsec_… ) you generate in the dashboard. It looks like this: Paystack-Signature: t = 1760270400 , v1 = whk_3f9a1c2e : 9d1b . . . e47a To verify it, per Paystack's docs: Read the raw body bytes before any JSON parsing. Take t and every v1 value ( <key id>:<signature> ). Reject events where t is more than 300 seconds from your server's time (replay protection). Compute HMAC-SHA512 of ${t}. + raw body, keyed with the whole whsec_… secret. Compare against each v1 signature in constant time. // lib/paystack-webhook.ts import "server-only" ; import { createHmac , timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto" ; const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 ; export function verifyPaystackSignature ( raw : Buffer , header : string | null , secret : string ) : boolean { if ( ! header ) return false ; let t : number | null = null ; const signatures : string [ ] = [ ] ; for ( const part of header . split ( "," ) ) { const i = part . indexOf ( "=" ) ; if ( i === - 1 ) continue ; const key = part . slice ( 0 , i ) . trim ( ) ; const value = part . slice ( i + 1 ) . trim ( ) ; if ( key === "t" && /^ \ d + $ / . test ( value ) ) t = Number ( value ) ; if ( key === "v1" ) { const j = value . indexOf ( ":" ) ; if ( j !== - 1 ) signatures . push ( value . slice ( j + 1 ) ) ; } } if ( t === null || signatures . length === 0 ) return false ; if ( Math . abs ( Date . now ( ) / 1000 - t ) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS ) return false ; const expected = createHmac ( "sha512" , secret ) . update ( `${t}.` ) . update ( raw ) . digest ( ) ; return signatures . some ( ( hex ) => /^ [ 0 - 9a - f ] { 128 } $ / . test ( hex ) && timingSafeEqual ( expected , Buffer . from ( hex , "hex" ) ) ) ; } And the route handler. In the App Router you get the raw body with req.arrayBuffer() ; don't call req.json() first, because re-serialising parsed JSON changes the bytes and the signature will never match. // app/api/paystack/webhook/route.ts import { after } from "next/server" ; import { fulfilOrder } from "@/lib/orders" ; import { verifyPaystackSignature } from "@/lib/paystack-webhook" ; export async function POST ( req : Request ) { const raw = Buffer . from ( await req . arrayBuffer ( ) ) ; const secret = process . env . PAYSTACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET ; if ( ! secret ) return new Response ( "Webhook secret not configured" , { status : 500 } ) ; if ( ! verifyPaystackSignature ( raw , req . headers . get ( "paystack-signature" ) , secret ) ) { return new Response ( "Invalid signature" , { status : 401 } ) ; } const event = JSON . parse ( raw . toString ( "utf8" ) ) ; if ( event . event === "charge.success" ) { // Acknowledge fast; do the work after the response is sent. after ( ( ) => fulfilOrder ( event . data . reference ) ) ; } return new Response ( null , { status : 200 } ) ; } A few production notes: Return 200 quickly. Paystack retries anything that isn't a 200 OK — in live mode every 3 minutes for the first 4 tries, then hourly for 72 hours. Long work belongs after the response, which is what after() is for. Return 200 for events you don't handle , too. Otherwise Paystack keeps retrying them. Still verify inside fulfilOrder . The signature proves the event came from Paystack; the verify call and amount check prove it matches your order. Older integrations may only receive the legacy x-paystack-signature header (HMAC-SHA512 of the raw body using your secret key, no timestamp). Paystack's advice is to keep verifying it until your events carry Paystack-Signature , and not to delete your secret key before then. Testing it locally Webhooks can't reach localhost . Expose your dev server with a tunnel (or the Paystack CLI), put that URL in the test webhook field in your dashboard, and make a payment with Paystack's test cards. Then deliberately close the tab right after paying: the order should still end up paid , by webhook. That one test catches most broken integrations. The checklist Secret key and webhook secret are server-only (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ ) Prices come from your database, in kobo, never from the client You generate and store the reference before initializing Every fulfilment path verifies status, amount and currency pending → paid happens in one conditional update (idempotent) Webhook verifies the signature on the raw body and returns 200 fast Tested: pay, then close the tab — order still fulfilled Payments are the one feature where "mostly works" means someone lost money. If you'd like a Paystack integration built or reviewed, that's one of the things I do — or just get in touch . Sources: Paystack: Accept Payments · Paystack: Webhooks · Paystack: Verify Payments

title: Why CSIR NET Part C Questions Are 2.3x Longer Than Part B: An Audit of 1,565 Practice Questions
summary: I built JRF Life , a free CSIR NET Life Science practice site, and recently analysed every question in its bank. Across all 1,565 questions , Part C questions average 421.7 characters , compared to 183.6 characters in Part B and 140.2 in Part A . ( Full method and topic table ) Candidates often practise unit MCQs without timers, then get surprised in the 180-minute NTA Computer Based Test (CBT) when 75 long, experiment-based Part C questions arrive with a -1.0 penalty for wrong answers. How Parts A, B and C differ Part A (77 questions, +2 / -0.5): 140.2 characters on average, 5.2% Advanced, all explained. Part B ([VERIFY: 750] questions, +2 / -0.5): 183.6 characters on average, 0% Advanced, all explained. Part C (738 questions, +4 / -1): 421.7 characters on average (2.3x Part B), 71.5% Advanced or Hard (528 questions), all explained. Enforcing the real section limits in TypeScript The real exam lets you attempt only 15 of 20 in Part A, 35 of 50 in Part B and 25 of 75 in Part C. The practice simulator on JRF Life enforces the same limits, so you have to choose which questions to answer: const PART_RULES = { a: { total: 20, maxAttempt: 15, correct: 2, penalty: 0.5 }, b: { total: 50, maxAttempt: 35, correct: 2, penalty: 0.5 }, c: { total: 75, maxAttempt: 25, correct: 4, penalty: 1.0 }, } as const Once you reach the limit, you have to deselect a low-confidence answer before choosing a new one. That mirrors the trade-off in the real exam. Try it See the full topic breakdown on the guide page , or check how wrong answers in Part C affect your score in the free calculator .

title: 1Password didn't get hacked by a genius. It got hacked by one GitHub login.
summary: I'll be honest, my first reaction to the 1Password news yesterday was "ok, time to move everything." Then I actually read what happened, and now I'm more annoyed at how it happened than worried about my passwords. Here's the whole thing in 30 seconds: Someone got into one employee's GitHub account They used it to push code to 1Password's backend That code quietly pulled customer records: names, emails, account IDs, sign-up date, last login A smaller group also had invite and recovery tokens taken from emails What they didn't get: vaults, passwords, Secret Keys, recovery keys. The encryption held, and that part is genuinely impressive. But think about it for a second. No zero-day, no nation-state wizardry. One developer login was enough to get code running against real customer data. My hot take: the encryption design saved 1Password here, not their internal security. If a single account can push to production without anyone else approving it, that's not a GitHub problem, that's a process problem. And I'd bet a lot of companies reading this have the exact same hole. The part that actually affects you and me: someone now has a clean list of confirmed 1Password users with their emails . Expect very convincing "unusual sign-in" or "complete your account recovery" emails over the next few weeks. If you didn't start it, don't click it. Open the app yourself. So I want to hear from you: Are you staying with 1Password? A) Staying, the vault held and that's what matters B) Moving to Bitwarden / Proton Pass / something else C) Going self-hosted, done trusting anyone's cloud And for the devs here: could one compromised GitHub account push code to production at your company today? Be honest 👀

title: Mem0 alternatives in 2026: Cognee, Korely, Letta, Supermemory, Zep
summary: This page compares Mem0 with five alternatives: Cognee, Korely, Letta, Supermemory and Zep. Cognee builds a knowledge graph from documents. Letta is a platform for building the whole agent. For facts that change, like a customer's plan, look at Zep, which puts four dates on every fact, and Korely, which gives the old fact an end date. Supermemory has a local install, and Mem0 has a free plan and an open-source library. The table puts them side by side on the points people ask about first: open source, self-hosting, free plans, where the data lives. Each cell about another product links its source, checked on 23 November 2026. Product Open source Self-hosting Free plan Where the data lives A fact that changes Cognee Apache 2.0 Runs locally, free, or in Docker Free tier Your machine; cloud region not stated Bi-temporal memory listed under Enterprise Korely Apache 2.0 With Docker Hobby plan Helsinki Old fact gets an end date; as_of reads a past day Letta Apache 2.0 letta server Free, 3 agents Letta Cloud or your machine Markdown files in git ( docs ) Mem0 Apache 2.0 Library or Docker server Free, monthly limits Mem0's servers Both kept, current ranked higher ( docs ) Supermemory MIT ; local server not public Local binary , up to 10,000 docs Free, 5 USD credits Managed cloud New fact replaces old for search ( docs ) Zep Graphiti is Apache 2.0 Graphiti, self-hosted only Free, 10,000 credits Managed Cloud Invalidated, not deleted; four dates ( docs ) Paid plans are on each pricing page. They change, so check the page. Which one for which job Cognee describes a knowledge graph built from documents, code and conversations , and runs locally for free with no API key. Korely keeps each fact with a start and an end date. One read gives you what holds today, another what held on a given day. Several agents can share one memory, and it runs on the Cloud or Self-hosted. Letta is for building an agent on a platform where memory is files in git, with shared memory between agents in Letta Cloud. Mem0 has an open-source library and a Docker server, a free hosted plan to try, and, on its Platform, four kinds of id to scope memory (user, agent, app, run). Supermemory has a dry-run preview before a forget by query , and offers a local binary for a single developer. Zep puts four dates on every fact and offers date filters on fact search . Graphiti, its open-source framework, suits you if you want to run a temporal graph yourself. Mem0 vs Zep When a fact changes, Mem0 and Zep both keep the old version, in different ways. Mem0's Platform keeps both and ranks the current one higher . Zep marks the old one invalidated, puts four dates on each fact and offers date filters on fact search . If you want a library, a Docker server or a hosted Platform that scopes memory by user, agent, app and run, that's Mem0. If you want four dates on each fact, or Graphiti to run that graph yourself, that's Zep. Mem0 vs Supermemory Start with the licences. Mem0's repository is Apache 2.0, Supermemory's main one is MIT, and its local server's source isn't in the public repository. For a changed fact, Supermemory lets the new one replace the old for search , with history that "can remain for audit". Before a forget by query, it shows a dry-run preview of what would go. So if you want to read the server's code, Mem0's is open under Apache 2.0, and if that preview matters more, Supermemory has it. Mem0 vs Letta These two are different kinds of product. Mem0 has an open-source library, a Docker server and a hosted Platform. Letta's docs describe a platform for building agents, where memory is Markdown files in a git repository, every edit committed . You run it with letta server , and its shared memory, kept in Letta Cloud, requires cloud-hosted agents . If you're building the whole agent, look at Letta. If you already have the agent and only need its memory, Mem0. Mem0 vs Cognee Cognee is the one to look at if your agent learns from documents. It builds a knowledge graph from documents, code and conversations and runs locally for free with no API key. Like Mem0, it's Apache 2.0 and runs on your own machine, and the two list a free plan on their pricing pages . Mem0 scopes memory by user, agent, app and run. Mem0 vs Korely On the basics they match: Apache 2.0 code, a hosted service with a free plan, and Docker for your own server. They part ways on a fact that changes. Mem0's Platform keeps both versions and ranks the current one higher. Korely gives the old one an end date, so a normal read returns only the current one, and as_of asks what was true on any past day ( Temporal facts ). What people check when they compare Mem0 Mem0 comes up a lot in this space, so it's the one many people compare against. I'd check four things, and Mem0's own pages say something on each. Facts that change. Mem0's v3 migration page says that when information changes, "both facts are preserved with temporal context", and retrieval ranks current information higher. If your agent quotes plans or prices, check how each layer tells today's fact from last month's. Facts extracted from text. Mem0 pulls facts out of the text your agent saves ( scoped memory ), and so does Korely ( Data governance ). Whatever you pick, save a week of your own conversations and read what it keeps. Cost. A memory layer is billed by use, so people want to know what a month looks like for their own agent. Mem0's pricing page lists a Free plan with monthly limits and a Custom plan, and says use beyond the free limits is billed by usage, with a monthly cap you set. Memory shared between agents. Mem0 keeps memory apart with four ids, for the user, the agent, the app and the run, and its scoped memory page explains which filter reads a user's facts and an agent's facts together (it says to use OR). If several of your agents will write about the same person, check how each layer lets them read each other's notes. Going by their public pages, Mem0, Zep and Supermemory all keep old facts in some form. Each tells today's fact from the old ones its own way, and the table below shows how. To find out which way fits your agent, I'd ask six questions. Six questions for any memory layer These are the six questions I'd put to any of them, Korely included. Most come with a short example you can swap for your own. Are facts dated? A shop your bot knows opened at nine and opens at eight since March. Can you see since when, and ask what the time was in February? What happens to the old fact? When "opens at eight" arrives, is "opens at nine" marked as ended, kept as if still current, or deleted? Can you correct a fact? The bot saved the wrong shoe size for a customer. Can you fix that one fact, and keep the wrong one as history? Can you delete a person? A customer asks you to erase what you hold about them. What does one call remove, and what stays? Can agents share it? A support agent and a delivery agent both talk to the same customer. Do they see each other's notes? Where does the data live? Which region, and can you run it yourself? The six questions, product by product The same checks in more detail, for the four products that keep facts for you. Question Korely Mem0 Supermemory Zep 1. Correcting a fact correct_fact , old one kept as history update overwrites Update the source document Edit not found; delete 4. Deleting a person delete_all ; backups up to 35 days delete_all(user_id) Delete the namespace Delete the user ; backups up to 365 days 5. Sharing between agents agent_id per agent, read by user_id ( post ) Four scopes, OR filter Namespaces Shared graphs , Context MCP 6. Where the data lives Helsinki , or self-hosted Mem0's servers , or self-host the library Managed cloud Managed Cloud , BYOK and BYOC If your case is a fact that changes, read the first two rows first. Cognee and Letta. They aren't in this table because their docs describe something different, as the blocks above say: a knowledge graph for Cognee, memory as files in git for Letta. Cognee also has a forget operation that removes specific items or datasets. I didn't find validity dates on facts for either of them, on the pages I read. Benchmarks. Each maker publishes its own scores with its own recipe and model, so they don't make one ranking; ours are in the README on GitHub . What I take home If I could keep only one question from these pages, it would be "which fact holds today?". Put it to any memory layer with a case of your own, like the shop's opening time, and when a page says nothing, ask the company. I build Korely, one of the products compared here. title: Building GPT-2 (124M) in PyTorch: weight parity, a speed ladder and about 150 GPU-minutes of my own training
summary: "I implemented GPT-2" can mean three very different things. You can load OpenAI's weights into your own code and show it computes the same function. You can make the training loop fast. Or you can start from random weights and train a model that actually learns something. All three happened in my repository neuron-to-gpt , my weekly submissions for a 12-week AI program that went from a single neuron to GPT-2. Keeping their numbers apart turned out to be harder than producing them. The GPT-2 weeks follow the outline of Andrej Karpathy's "Let's reproduce GPT-2 (124M)" lecture, so the model itself will look familiar. This post is about what I added around it: a full-logit parity test on English, Turkish and emoji prompts that guards the weight import, a speed ladder where every stage is timed on its own and the flash stage cannot silently fall back, a resumable training run with its interruption written into the record, and a paired comparison against GPT-2 on a held-out HellaSwag cohort. TL;DR Stage What it is Headline number What it proves Week 10 My GPT-2 holding OpenAI's weights max logit diff 5.3e-05 to 8.4e-05 on an A100 (rtol = atol = 1e-4 per logit) my code computes the reference function Week 11 Cumulative speed stages on an L4 53.75 → 36.23 ms per update, 1.48× which change actually helped, at one small shape Week 12 Random init, 60 min on an NVIDIA L4 validation NLL 11.01 → 4.98; HellaSwag 27.6% my training pipeline learns G4 That checkpoint, 90 more minutes on an RTX PRO 6000 NLL 4.98 → 3.67; HellaSwag 27.6% → 32.3% on the first 1,000 examples, 30.5% vs GPT-2's 33.7% on a held-out 1,000 real progress; below GPT-2 on both cohorts' point estimates The model Standard GPT-2 small: 12 blocks, 12 heads, width 768, 1,024 positions, pre-LayerNorm, tanh-approximate GELU, learned absolute positions and a fused Q/K/V projection. The token embedding and the output layer share one matrix (weight tying), which saves 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376 parameters: the tied model has 124,439,808 unique parameters, the untied one would have 163,037,184. Initialization follows GPT-2: std 0.02 for weight matrices, and std 0.02/√(2L) for the two residual output projections in each block. Every block adds two contributions to the residual stream, so without the smaller scale the variance of the stream grows with depth. Week 10: weight parity is a correctness test, not training To check the implementation, I import the published OpenAI weights (the Hugging Face copy, pinned to a fixed revision) into my own modules and compare outputs. The trap is in the import. Hugging Face's GPT-2 uses a historical Conv1D layer that stores weights as (input, output). nn.Linear expects (output, input). So four weight matrices per block must be transposed. For three of them a forgotten transpose fails loudly with a shape error. The attention output projection is 768 × 768, so a missing transpose there loads without complaint and silently computes a different function. From load_hf_weights in week10/model.py : transposed_suffixes = ( ".attn.c_attn.weight" , ".attn.c_proj.weight" , ".mlp.c_fc.weight" , ".mlp.c_proj.weight" , ) . . . tensor = source [ name ] . t ( ) if name . endswith ( transposed_suffixes ) else source [ name ] destination . copy_ ( tensor ) The loader validates every key and every shape before copying anything, so a late mismatch cannot leave a half-loaded model behind. The parity check compares full logits, not a sample. Both models get the same input in FP32, with eager attention, TF32 off and dropout off, and every logit must agree within rtol = atol = 1e-4. I used three prompts on purpose: an English sentence, a Turkish one, and a mixed string with an emoji, so that multi-byte BPE paths are exercised too. On an A100 the largest absolute difference per prompt was between 5.3e-05 and 8.4e-05, and all three passed; the same check also passed on a T4. That proves my code computes the same function as the reference when it holds the same weights. It says nothing about whether my code can learn. For that, Week 10 has a deliberately narrow diagnostic: 300 updates on one fixed batch (4 × 32 tokens) from random weights. Loss went from 11.056 to about 0.0001 and token accuracy reached 100%. That is memorization of a single batch. It shows gradients flow and the optimizer steps; it is not evidence of generalization, and I never report it as such. Week 11: a speed ladder where every rung is measured The question for Week 11 was simple: which of the usual speed-ups actually helps on the GPU I have? Instead of switching everything on at once, each stage is added on top of the previous one and timed separately. Stage (cumulative) Median ms / update Tokens/s vs previous baseline, FP32, eager attention 53.750 4,762.8 1.000× + TF32 matmul 53.043 4,826.3 1.013× + BF16 autocast 59.097 4,331.9 0.898× + torch.compile 36.790 6,958.4 1.606× + SDPA, flash kernel only 36.171 7,077.4 1.017× + vocabulary padded to 50,304 36.227 7,066.6 0.998× The conditions matter as much as the numbers: B = 2, T = 128, 5 warmup updates, 20 timed updates per stage, one run, on an NVIDIA L4. Each timed update includes data transfer, forward, backward, unscale/clip and the AdamW step, with a CUDA synchronization per step. Compile time and warmup are excluded (compilation plus warmup took about 42 seconds for that stage). What I took from it: The torch.compile stage was the largest single step: 1.606× on top of the TF32 and BF16 stages. The whole ladder came to 1.48× against the FP32 baseline. Compile was not measured in isolation, so part of that step may simply be recovering what the BF16 stage lost. BF16 autocast made things slower here (0.898×). I did not profile why. At B = 2, T = 128 the step is small enough that overheads can outweigh faster math, but that is a hypothesis, not a measurement. Either way it is a fact about this shape on an L4, not about mixed precision in general, and it is exactly the kind of result that disappears if you only compare "everything on" with "everything off". No fake FlashAttention. The flash stage runs inside sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.FLASH_ATTENTION) , which disallows the math and memory-efficient fallbacks. If the flash kernel cannot run, the stage fails instead of quietly measuring something else under the flash label. Vocabulary padding showed no measurable gain in this single run (0.998×). Padding 50,257 to 50,304 (a multiple of 64) is a common trick; I would need repeated runs to say more. The padded model has 124,475,904 parameters, and the 47 extra classes are implementation-only: they are excluded from sampling and from evaluation. Gradient accumulation also gets a correctness rule: K micro-batches with equal token counts each contribute loss / K, so the summed gradient equals the gradient of the mean loss over the combined batch. Clipping and the AdamW step happen once per update, after unscaling. Week 12: a real dataset, from random weights Week 12 is a separate model. It starts from random weights, not from OpenAI's. Data pipeline Source: FineWeb-Edu sample-10BT , pinned to a fixed dataset revision, so the run can be traced back to exact documents. Split by document, not by token. Validation documents are filled first and never appear in training; exact duplicates are removed. Near-duplicate cleaning and benchmark contamination scans were not done, and the report says so. Budget in tokens, not documents: 20,000,000 training tokens in 20 shards and a 131,072-token validation shard, all counted with the GPT-2 tokenizer, with an end-of-text token at each document boundary. Storage: 1M-token uint16 NPY shards, each with a SHA-256 in the manifest. The loader memory-maps the shards and builds windows that cross shard boundaries, so no tail of a shard is silently dropped. Fixed validation: every check measures exactly the same first 32 batches = 32,768 target tokens. A validation number that moves because the slice moved is worthless. Training setup B = 4, T = 256, accumulation 4 (4,096 tokens per update), BF16, SDPA, torch.compile , a 100-update warmup and a 60-minute wall-clock budget. The checkpoint ( last.pt ) stores not just weights but the AdamW and scaler state, the data loader position and the RNG state, so a Colab disconnect does not silently restart the data stream or the schedule. The run made 19,586 updates and processed 80,224,256 tokens in 60.20 minutes. Validation NLL went from 11.013 to 4.984965. HellaSwag, done carefully HellaSwag gives a context and four endings; the model picks the ending it finds most likely. Small protocol choices move the score by points, so I pinned all of them: Dataset: the deprecated GitHub JSONL URL now returns 404, so I use Rowan/hellaswag from the Hugging Face Hub, pinned to a revision. Scoring: only the ending tokens are scored, using mean token NLL (acc_norm). The context is encoded once, each ending is encoded separately with its leading space, and nothing is cleaned up. Long contexts are left-trimmed by the same amount for all four endings, so no ending gets an advantage from extra context. Same vocabulary for both models: logits are sliced to the 50,257 real GPT-2 IDs, removing my model's 47 padding classes before the softmax. Same numerics: FP32, TF32 off, for my model and for OpenAI GPT-2 (weights pinned to a revision and loaded into my own implementation). losses = F . cross_entropy ( logits [ . . . , : 50257 ] . float ( ) . reshape ( - 1 , min ( 50257 , logits . shape [ - 1 ] ) ) , targets . reshape ( - 1 ) , reduction = "none" ) . reshape_as ( targets ) totals = ( losses * mask ) . sum ( - 1 ) # mask: ending positions only means = totals / mask . sum ( - 1 ) # acc_norm uses the mean On the first 1,000 validation examples, my 60-minute model scored 27.6% (chance is 25%). OpenAI GPT-2, under the identical protocol, scored 33.6%. Eighty million tokens is a small experiment, not a pretraining reproduction; a gap is expected, though this run does not isolate its causes. A note on the absolute numbers. Karpathy's build-nanogpt script, with the same completion-style acc_norm, reports 29.55% for GPT-2 124M on all 10,042 validation examples. My 1,000-example slices give GPT-2 33.6% and 33.7%, and the Wilson interval for 33.6% (about 30.7% to 36.6%) does not reach 29.55%. So the first 2,000 examples of the pinned Rowan/hellaswag split look easier than the full set, or something in the data source differs; I did not run the full set to find out. The scores in this post are therefore comparable with each other, under one protocol and on the same indices, and not with published full-set numbers. G4: continuing my own checkpoint on a bigger GPU The last experiment takes that exact L4 checkpoint, verifies its hash, and continues training on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU for 90 minutes. It is not started from OpenAI weights. Settings: B = 8, T = 1,024, accumulation 4 (32,768 tokens per update), BF16, SDPA, torch.compile and fused AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95), ε = 1e-8, weight decay 0.1 on matrices and gradient clipping at 1.0. The learning rate warms up over 30 successful updates and then follows a cosine envelope tied to wall-clock time, from 3e-4 down to 3e-5, so the schedule ends when the budget ends regardless of throughput. Fresh data, checked against the old run. A new 200M-token training pool was drawn from the same pinned FineWeb-Edu revision. Every document whose SHA-256 exactly matches a document in the earlier L4 training or validation set was removed. The 131,072-token validation shard was carried over byte for byte, so the L4 and G4 validation numbers measure the same 32,768 targets. Resume bookkeeping is part of the result. The first session was planned against a clock deadline. It was interrupted after 3,989 committed updates and resumed from the verified checkpoint; on resume the deadline-based limit was removed and the total budget across both sessions set to 90 minutes (the pause between sessions is not counted). The 3,989 updates were kept and 16,384 tokens from an unfinished micro-batch were read again. The source version, the old and new budget settings and the checkpoint hash are all recorded under resumes in training.json . A loss curve without its resume history is hard to trust. Result: 38,061 updates, 1,247,182,848 processed tokens, 90.01 minutes, about 230,933 tokens/s over wall time. Validation NLL fell from 4.984965 to 3.665616. Two caveats travel with those numbers. Processed tokens are not unique data: the 200M-token pool was seen about 6.24 times. And the throughput is not a controlled comparison with the L4 run, because context length, batch, data and hardware all changed. Two HellaSwag cohorts, chosen before looking Evaluation L4 checkpoint G4 continuation OpenAI GPT-2 FineWeb validation NLL (fixed 32,768 targets) 4.984965 3.665616 not measured HellaSwag, indices 0–999 27.6% 32.3% 33.6% HellaSwag, indices 1,000–1,999 not measured 30.5% 33.7% Indices 0–999 were already used in Week 12, so they only show continuity: the same examples went from 27.6% to 32.3%. Indices 1,000–1,999 were reserved in advance as the main comparison, and the checkpoint was selected by validation loss, never by HellaSwag. On that held-out cohort my model scores 30.5% and GPT-2 33.7%. Both models answer the same questions, so I compare them pairwise instead of treating the two accuracies as independent: Cohort Only mine correct Only GPT-2 correct Paired bootstrap 95% CI (mine − GPT-2) Exact McNemar p 0–999 88 101 [−4.00, +1.40] points 0.383 1,000–1,999 58 90 [−5.60, −0.80] points 0.0106 The bootstrap uses 20,000 resamples with seed 20261108 and assumes independent examples, so it is a rough uncertainty measure. Read plainly: on the first cohort the data cannot separate the two models; on the held-out cohort GPT-2 is ahead. There is no equivalence claim to make, and nothing here says anything about chat, code or reasoning. What the text looks like Same prompt, seed 42, temperature 0.8, top-k 50, at most 48 new tokens. At the start of G4: The children walked into the way, which is called the "Kak," they take into account their own needs and can be taught in the form of "Rarm," ... At the end of G4: The children walked into the school and enjoyed the music. As the summer started to get underway, the teacher was amazed at the new songs. A young man was still amazed by the songs. ... The sentences are better formed, but the model still repeats itself and loses the thread a few lines later. One sample is an illustration, not an evaluation. Lessons I would apply to any training project Compare full logits, not shapes. A missing transpose on the square attention projection passes a shape check. Include non-ASCII text so multi-byte BPE paths are exercised too. Measure optimizations one at a time. The ladder showed BF16 slowing things down at a small shape and the torch.compile stage as the largest single step (1.606× on top of TF32 and BF16). An all-on versus all-off comparison would have hidden both. Make silent fallbacks impossible. If the flash kernel is not allowed to fall back, a flash number really is a flash number. Pin everything that can drift. Dataset revision, model revision, the validation slice, the HellaSwag source, the scoring code. Otherwise a later number is not comparable to an earlier one. Choose the held-out set before you look. It is the reason I treat 30.5% as the result and 32.3% as continuity. Keep claims apart in the repository, not only in the prose. Week 10 imports weights to verify code; Week 12 starts from random; G4 continues Week 12; OpenAI GPT-2 is only an evaluation reference. Limits Week 12 and G4 are single runs. I did not measure seed-to-seed variance. G4 processed 1.25B tokens but only 200M unique ones (about 6.24 passes), so its token count overstates the data it saw. I did not compare against a no-repeat run. HellaSwag was run on two 1,000-example slices, not on the full 10,042-example set. GPU inference was not rerun locally. I verified the exported file hashes, the token and update accounting, and the predictions reconstructed from the saved per-example NLL scores. Rerunning G4 needs my backed-up checkpoint and token shards. A fresh clone contains the evidence, not the weights. G4 run environment: PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.13.16. Requirements use version ranges, not a lockfile. This is a base language model study, not a chat assistant or a production service. The evidence check runs without a GPU, a checkpoint or a dataset download: git clone https://github.com/muend/neuron-to-gpt cd neuron-to-gpt python experiments/g4/analyze_results.py --check The check recomputes file hashes, token and update accounting, and the correct counts from the saved per-example NLL scores; it does not rerun the model. The G4 report and its per-example evaluation files are in experiments/g4/results/nvidia_rtx_pro6000/ , the speed ladder in week11/results/nvidia_l4/ , and the parity report in week10/results/ . The Week 12 README lists build-nanogpt's HellaSwag script as the reference evaluation protocol. If you spot a flaw in the evaluation setup, I would like to hear about it in the comments.

title: Free AI coding terminal for students: Mel with a free API key
summary: Students can code with AI agents for $0. Mel – the agentic terminal (openmel.dev) is free on Mac, Windows and Linux when you bring your own API key, and Groq and Google AI Studio both give free keys. Put the two together and you have a terminal with a team of AI agents that plans, writes, runs and tests code, at no cost. This guide shows how to set it up in ten minutes, what the free keys can and cannot do, and how to use it for class projects and hackathons. Is there a free AI coding tool for students? Yes. Mel's Free plan costs $0, and every agent turn on your own key costs 0 Mel credits. The only thing an AI agent needs to run is a model, and two providers give model keys with a free tier: What it is Cost Mel – the agentic terminal A terminal with a team of AI agents built in $0 on the Free plan Groq key Fast open models (GPT-OSS, Qwen) Free tier, limited per minute and per day Google AI Studio key Gemini models Free tier, limited per minute and per day Set it up in ten minutes Download Mel for Mac, Windows or Linux and open it. Get a free key from Groq or Google AI Studio . Our free key guide walks through both. Sign in to Mel with a free account. The terminal works without one; the AI agent needs it. Paste the key. Click your avatar, choose Settings , open AI , scroll to Provider API keys , paste the key and click Save . Ask the agent. Press Ctrl+Enter (⌘↵ on a Mac) and describe a task with a clear finish line, like "make a Flask app with a login page and a test for wrong passwords." Each answer ends with a usage line. On your own key it reads "0 credits · your key". What the free keys can and cannot do Free keys are a great way to learn, but read the terms: Groq's free plan is limited by requests and tokens per minute and per day, per model. If you hit the limit, wait or switch models. Google's free Gemini tier lets Google use what you send to improve its products, and human reviewers may read it. Do not send private or sensitive code on it. Google's terms say only paid services may be offered to users in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK. For a class project or a hackathon, both are usually enough. For an internship or company code, use a paid key. Use it for class projects Start from a clear task. Say what should change, which files to read, what "done" means and the command that checks it. Our task checklist shows how. Read every change before you keep it. Open View changes and go through the diff. You learn more, and you catch the agent's mistakes. Let it run the tests. An agent that can run pytest or npm test catches its own errors before you do. Follow your school's rules on AI use. Mel is a tool; your work is still yours to understand and explain. Use it at a hackathon At a hackathon, time is the scarce thing. With Mel you can split the work: one agent builds the front end, another the API, and you review both. On a paid plan, /orchestrate-agent puts several Mel agents on one task; the Free plan runs one Mel agent at a time. If your team already uses Claude Code or Codex, type claude or codex in a Mel tab and each opens as a full session. Mel runs hackathons and build nights with students at Miami Dade College, plus the online Global AI Hackathon. See events for what is next, and community to start a Mel group at your school. FAQ Is there a free AI coding terminal for students? Yes. Mel – the agentic terminal is free on Mac, Windows and Linux with your own API key, and Groq and Google AI Studio give free keys. Does it work on a Windows laptop? Yes. Mel runs on Windows, Mac and Linux, and has a VS Code extension. Can I use it at hackathons? Yes. You can run Claude Code or Codex in Mel tabs side by side, and on a paid plan several Mel agents can work on one task. Is my code private on a free key? It depends on the provider. Google's free tier may be used to improve its products and read by reviewers. Groq says it does not keep inference requests by default except to troubleshoot or investigate abuse. title: Real-Time Voice Translation Just Went Mainstream — Apple, Google, DeepL and $349 Earbuds
summary: A few years ago, live voice translation was a demo you watched on stage: a presenter speaks English, a pause, a robotic voice answers in Japanese, and the audience applauds the future. This week, it quietly became something else — a feature already sitting in the earbuds millions of people own. DeepL launched Aure v2 today, November 26, cutting the delay of its live voice translation in half. But the bigger story isn't one launch. It's that Apple, Google, DeepL and a wave of dedicated earbuds all landed on the same idea within about fourteen months — and the cheapest way in now costs less than a takeaway. I've been tracking this space since DeepL's first Aure launch two weeks ago, and the pattern is now clear enough to call it: real-time voice translation has gone mainstream. Here's what changed, how each option actually works, and which one fits you. What changed this week DeepL's Aure v2 is the news hook, and it's a real step: a new end-to-end speech-to-speech model that skips the old transcribe-translate-synthesise relay entirely. Median translation delay is 50% lower than Aure v1, which only launched on November 11. Six languages at launch — English, German, French, Spanish, Japanese and Korean — auto-enabled for DeepL Voice customers. I wrote up the details separately, because the architecture change deserves its own space. But Aure v2 is the professional end of the spectrum. The reason I'm calling this a wave rather than a launch is what's happening on the consumer side at the same time. Apple: translation in the earbuds you may already own Apple's Live Translation arrived in September 2025 with iOS 26 and the AirPods Pro 3. Someone speaks French or Japanese; you hear it in English in your ears, with a transcript in the Translate app. The honest details: it runs on the iPhone, not inside the earbuds. You need an iPhone 15 Pro or later with Apple Intelligence switched on, plus supported AirPods — Pro 2 or 3, AirPods 4 with noise cancellation, AirPods 5, or AirPods Max 2. Nine languages are covered (eleven variants, counting US and UK English and both forms of Mandarin Chinese). Apple still labels it beta. One correction worth making: the EU didn't get it at launch. It arrived there in December 2025 with iOS 26.2, after a delay Apple attributed to the Digital Markets Act. If you read an old article saying it doesn't work in Europe, that's out of date. Who it fits: iPhone owners who travel or take calls across languages and don't want another device, another app, or another subscription. If you already own the hardware, it costs nothing extra. Google: any headphones, 70+ languages Google's answer is the most open one, and in some ways the most interesting. Live Translate in the Google Translate app turns any pair of headphones — Bluetooth or wired, any brand — into a live translator. The phone's microphone picks up the speaker, Gemini processes the speech, and you hear the translation in your ears. It preserves tone, emphasis and cadence, according to Google, so you can follow who said what, not just what was said. The numbers: more than 70 languages, powered by Gemini 2.5 Flash Native Audio. It started as a beta on Android in December 2025 in the US, Mexico and India, then expanded to iPhone and nine more countries in March 2026 — including the UK, Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Japan, Nigeria, Bangladesh and Thailand. There are two modes, and the distinction matters. Continuous listening is for one-way situations — a lecture, a conference talk, a broadcast. Two-way conversation mode handles a dialogue, detecting which language is being spoken and switching the output automatically. Who it fits: almost everyone else. Android users obviously, but also iPhone owners who don't want to be locked to Apple's nine languages, and anyone who wants the widest language coverage for free. The catch is the obvious one: it's cloud processing, so it needs a connection, and it's still labelled beta in places. The dedicated earbuds: Timekettle and the $349 tier Then there's the hardware built for one job. Timekettle's W4 AI Interpreter Earbuds, launched at IFA 2025 in September, are the flagship of this category: 42 languages and 95 accents, a bone-voiceprint sensor that picks up speech vibrations from your jawbone to cut through background noise, and LLM-powered translation that tries to tell phonetically similar phrases apart. Price: $349, with a $449 Pro model aimed at professional interpreters. Timekettle claims 98% accuracy and 0.2-second lag. Those are the company's own numbers — no independent test backs them yet — but the hardware idea is genuinely clever: in a noisy market or a crowded station, a microphone that reads your jawbone has a real advantage over one that reads the room. Who it fits: frequent travellers, tour guides, and anyone who has regular face-to-face conversations in noisy places. If your use case is a quiet video call, the phone in your pocket already does this for free. The budget end: $6 earbuds and a warning label Here's where the wave gets strange. Scroll TikTok Shop or Shopee and you'll find AI translation earbuds for $6 to $50, some claiming 133 languages or more. They sell in huge volumes. And some of them genuinely work — after a fashion — because most of them are just a microphone, a Bluetooth chip, and an app that does the real work on your phone. But the claims need a warning label. "133 languages" on a $12 listing is a vendor claim, not a verified fact; many of these listings count dialects, reuse the same translation engine, and quote lag figures no reviewer has measured. The hardware is cheap; the translation quality is whatever the app behind it delivers, and that app is usually a white-label wrapper around a mainstream engine. My honest take: if you want to try the category for the price of a coffee, a cheap pair is a fun experiment. If you need it to work in a meeting that matters, don't trust a listing page — trust the three names above. The quiet one: offline translation One more thread worth knowing about. Not everything needs the cloud. Plamo 3 Translate runs translation on your own hardware, offline — no connection, no server, no data leaving the device. It's the opposite end of the spectrum from Google's cloud model, and it matters for classrooms, hospitals and anywhere with no signal or strict privacy rules. I covered it in more detail on ToolsDig, and it's the option most people overlook. Which one should you actually use? It depends on what you already own and where you'll use it: You have an iPhone 15 Pro or newer and supported AirPods: try Apple's Live Translation first. It's free, it's already there, and nine languages cover most travel and business pairs. You want the most languages, on any headphones: Google's Live Translate, in the Translate app. 70+ languages, works with the earbuds you already own, free. You need it for business calls and meetings: DeepL Aure v2, if you're already a DeepL Voice customer — the delay cut and voice preservation are built for that room. My full write-up is here. You talk face-to-face in noisy places, often: a dedicated pair like the Timekettle W4. The bone-voiceprint sensor is a real hardware advantage, not a software trick. You're curious and your budget is tiny: a budget pair is a cheap experiment — just treat the language count on the listing as marketing, not a spec sheet. You need it offline or private: look at on-device options like Plamo 3 Translate. What I'm watching next Three things. First, language counts: Apple's nine languages are the obvious gap — Arabic, Hindi and Russian are all missing, and Google's 70+ makes that gap visible. Second, latency claims: every vendor quotes a number, nobody publishes an independent measurement, and a real head-to-head test of delay in a live conversation is overdue. Third, the offline question: as on-device models get better, the cloud dependency that all of these except Plamo share starts to look like a weakness, not a given. The Babelfish moment — the old sci-fi idea of a fish in your ear that translates everything — hasn't quite arrived. But for the first time, it's not a demo on a stage. It's a feature in the earbuds already in your pocket, in the app already on your phone, or in a $349 pair you can buy today. The question isn't whether live translation works anymore. It's which version of it you're already carrying. Sources: DeepL via PRNewswire, "DeepL Introduces Aure v2" (November 26, 2026); Apple AirPods Pro 3 product page and Live Translation support documentation; Google Translate Live Translate rollout coverage (December 2025 beta; March 2026 iOS expansion); Timekettle W4 launch coverage, IFA 2025 (PRNewswire, September 5, 2025). Vendor figures — Timekettle's 98% accuracy and 0.2s lag, budget-earbud language counts — are the vendors' own claims, not independently verified. No affiliate links in this article. title: Introducing BenchSaaS: Can LLMs Actually Deliver Inside Enterprise Software?
summary: Why "Done!" in a chat window isn't enough — and what 8,850 live runs across CRM, inventory, and finance reveal about today's leading AI models. Most LLM benchmarks test how well a model writes isolated code, solves competition math, or answers multiple-choice trivia. Those evaluations are useful, but they miss the question every CIO, product leader, and enterprise architect actually cares about: When you put an AI model inside live business software, can it finish real operational work without silently corrupting your database? To answer that question with evidence rather than demos, the Nocoly & Mingdao AI Tech Group built BenchSaaS V1.0 — an enterprise application LLM benchmark grounded in real CRM, inventory, procurement, and finance workflows. Built on Live Enterprise Software, Not Toy Mocks BenchSaaS runs on an isomorphic testbed built on Nocoly HAP (Hyper Application Platform) . Instead of synthetic single-API stubs, models operate inside two interconnected business applications — Procurement & Sales (32 tables) and Finance Management (8 tables) — totaling 40 structured business tables and 18,014 real-world business records , complete with relational links, workflow constraints, and audit logs. For the V1.0 evaluation (conducted October 22 – November 19, 2026), BenchSaaS evaluated: 100 real-world enterprise tasks sampled from a 500-task pool across Inventory & Procurement (52) , Finance & Accounting (27) , CRM (20) , and Cross-App tracing (1) — split between 60 read-only lookup/analysis tasks and 40 write or refusal tasks (16 record creations, 20 updates, and 4 refusal/no-change scenarios). 10 leading LLMs across 3 reasoning tiers ( Low , Mid , and High ), producing 30 distinct model configurations . 9,000 planned runs (3 repeats per task per configuration), yielding 8,850 valid runs ( 7,987 PASS , 863 FAIL , with 150 INVALID infrastructure runs tracked separately). Realistic execution guardrails: every run operated under hard limits of 31 turns, 30 tool calls, and a 1,800-second timeout, with automated database restoration between write runs. The Two-Gate Verification That Catches "Polite Failures" Anyone who has piloted AI agents in ERP or CRM workflows knows the most dangerous failure mode isn't a crash — it's a confident, well-written reply claiming a task is finished when the underlying record is broken. BenchSaaS enforces two mandatory verification gates : Gate 1 ( ANSWER_MATCH ): Evaluates the model's written response across all 100 tasks for factual accuracy, calculation correctness, citations, and mandatory write receipts. Gate 2 ( RESULT_CONSISTENCY ): On write tasks, reads back the frozen HAP database snapshot after execution — combining programmatic checks with an independent judge — to verify that every required field, status option, and cross-table relation was actually persisted and matches the model's claim. The results proved why backend verification is non-negotiable: 100% of the 165 Gate-2 database failures in BenchSaaS V1.0 had already passed Gate 1. In every single one of those 165 failures, the model's chat response sounded complete and trustworthy — yet the database snapshot revealed NULL fields, wrong entity codes written into the wrong columns, empty status arrays ( [] ), or values contradicting the model's own summary. In one representative Inventory task (Case 7.4: creating a draft purchase requisition), a model passed Gate 1 and created both the requisition header and line item — yet Gate 2 caught that the mandatory "Available Stock" field had been stored as NULL instead of 20 . Across all 30 configurations, only 44.32% of valid runs passed that task cleanly. Five Takeaways From 8,850 Live Enterprise Runs 1. Strong overall capability — and "Mid" reasoning often beats "High" Across all 8,850 valid runs, models achieved an aggregate solve rate of 90.25% . The top five configurations overall were: #1 Gemini 3.8 Flash (Mid): 97.94% (285/291) · 95.74% 3-of-3 repeat consistency · CNY ¥0.5476/run #2 Gemini 3.8 Flash (High): 97.24% (282/290) · CNY ¥0.7519/run #3 Kimi K3.1 Pro (High): 96.99% (290/299 — highest raw pass count out of 300 planned runs) · CNY ¥0.9273/run #4 DeepSeek V4 Pro (Mid): 96.96% (287/296) · CNY ¥0.9430/run #5 DeepSeek V4 Pro (Low): 96.25% (282/293) · CNY ¥0.8756/run (As the report notes, narrow rank margins should not be over-interpreted given small differences in valid run counts across configurations.) Crucially, turning reasoning effort all the way up did not reliably improve results. While GPT-6-Luna (73.13% → 92.23%), GLM-5.3 (81.82% → 94.54%), and Kimi K3.1 Pro (88.22% → 96.99%) gained significantly at higher tiers, Gemini 3.8 Flash , DeepSeek V4 Pro , and Qwen 3.8 Max all peaked at Mid , and MiniMax M3.1 Flash actually declined at High (79.79% → 76.41%). 2. No single model wins every business domain Enterprise accuracy varies sharply by domain — and different models lead different departments: CRM (95.31% average): Six configurations achieved a 100.00% solve rate ( Kimi K3.1 Pro High , Qwen 3.8 Max Mid , GPT-6-Luna High & Mid , and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Low & High ). Inventory & Procurement (90.02% average): Led by GPT-6.1-Terra (Low) at 98.72% (154/156), narrowly ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) (98.08%) and (Mid) (98.04%). Finance & Accounting (86.56% average — the toughest domain): Led by DeepSeek V4 Pro (Low) at 100.00% (76/76), followed by DeepSeek V4 Pro (Mid) (98.75%) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Mid) (98.67%). 3. Document creation exposes a ~20-point capability cliff Break the 100 tasks down by operational type, and a clear divide emerges. Models excelled at Workflow Tracing (95.35%) , Data Maintenance (95.19%) , and Audit & Reconciliation (95.12%) , and performed solidly on Decision Support (92.29%) , Data Aggregation (88.71%) , and Record Retrieval (84.89%) . Then came Document Creation , where the aggregate solve rate plunged to 76.99% . Creating a multi-table business document — a valid header, complete line items, correct relational links, and compliant status fields — remains the single sharpest differentiator in enterprise AI delivery ( Gemini 3.8 Flash swept the top three spots in Document Creation at 98.2%, 96.4%, and 96.4%). 4. Enterprise failures follow predictable engineering patterns Analyzing all 863 failed runs revealed four dominant root causes: Required Assertion Failures (68.71%, 593 runs): 428 Gate-1 answer gaps and 165 Gate-2 database integrity failures. Business Rule Rejections (18.66%, 161 runs): Attempting to write disallowed or read-only fields, or passing shorthand worksheet aliases instead of valid 24-character table IDs. Invalid Tool Arguments (5.91%, 51 runs): Failing schema validation twice in a row without self-correcting. Tool Budget Exhaustion (5.21%, 45 runs): Hitting the 30-call cap — and notably, 86.7% (39/45) of these runs had zero tool errors, simply burning their budget on brute-force pagination or repetitive lookups. 5. A 134× cost spread makes accuracy-only leaderboards obsolete Across all valid runs, median task latency was 86.55 seconds (ranging from 48.75s for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Low to 198.01s for Qwen 3.8 Max · High ), while mean cost per run was CNY ¥0.7111 — spanning 134× from ¥0.0241 ( GPT-6-Luna · Low , 73.13%) to ¥3.2358 ( Claude Sonnet 5.5 · High , 92.00%). That spread opens up compelling production tiers depending on your workload: Highest accuracy & repeat stability: Gemini 3.8 Flash · Mid (97.94% solve rate, 95.74% 3-of-3 repeat consistency, ¥0.5476/run). 90%+ high-efficiency value picks: GPT-6-Luna · Mid (90.97% at just ¥0.0302/run ) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Mid (92.23% at ¥0.1003/run and 57.03s median latency). Fastest 90%+ execution: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash · Low (90.91% in 48.75s median at ¥0.0809/run). What This Means for Teams Deploying Enterprise AI If you are building or adopting AI agents inside operational systems, BenchSaaS V1.0 points to three immediate design rules: Never trust verbal completion. Pair every write-capable agent with programmatic post-write verification against actual database state. Route by workflow, not hype. Domain leaders diverge across CRM, inventory, and finance, and "Mid" reasoning frequently outperforms "High" while running faster and cheaper. Evaluate the full delivery triangle. Accuracy alone is misleading without 3-of-3 repeat stability, latency, and per-task unit economics. Explore the Interactive Leaderboard & Full 51-Page Report BenchSaaS V1.0 is live now. You can filter the interactive leaderboard by domain, task type, reasoning tier, latency, and cost on the BenchSaaS V1.0 Landing Page , or download the complete 51-Page English Benchmark Report (PDF) for free. Are you a foundation model developer looking to inspect failure diagnostics on the public task suite, or a model service provider interested in supporting future benchmark rounds? title: How to add an MCP server to Codex (config.toml and codex mcp add)
summary: How to add an MCP server to Codex Checked against the official docs: Oct 27, 2026 Codex (the CLI, the IDE extension and the desktop app) can use MCP servers to reach tools and data beyond your repository. You add one either with a single codex mcp add command or by editing config.toml , and all Codex surfaces share the same configuration. This guide covers both, with examples built from OpenAI's documentation. Quick answer Run codex mcp add <name> -- <command> <args> . For example codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp (the example OpenAI's docs use). Run codex mcp list to confirm it is saved. Start codex and type /mcp to see the active servers. The command writes a [mcp_servers.<name>] table into ~/.codex/config.toml . You can edit that file directly for anything the command does not cover. The IDE extension and desktop app also have an MCP servers screen (in settings) that edits the same configuration. Where the config lives Global: ~/.codex/config.toml (on Windows, in .codex under your user folder). Project: .codex/config.toml in a project, which Codex reads for trusted projects only. The ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI and the IDE extension share this configuration, so you set a server up once. ChatGPT on the web does not read your local Codex files; it uses plugins instead. Option 1: codex mcp add The general form from OpenAI's docs codex mcp add < server-name > --env VAR1 = VALUE1 --env VAR2 = VALUE2 -- < stdio server-command > Everything after -- is the command that starts the server. Put --env options before it. A few real examples, using servers listed on PluginStack: # Context7: current library docs (example from the OpenAI docs) codex mcp add context7 -- npx -y @upstash/context7-mcp # Official Memory server codex mcp add memory -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory # Official Filesystem server: the last argument is the folder it may access codex mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem $HOME /projects See Context7 , Memory and Filesystem . The official TypeScript servers need Node 24 or newer from v2 onward ( what changed ). Other commands codex mcp list shows the configured servers. codex mcp --help lists all MCP commands. codex mcp login <server-name> starts the OAuth login for a server that supports it. A remote (HTTP) server For a hosted server, pass its address with --url instead of a command: Then run: codex mcp login example (if the server uses OAuth) codex mcp add example --url https://mcp.example.com Option 2: edit config.toml Each server is a [mcp_servers.<name>] table. For a local (stdio) server, command is required; args , env , env_vars and cwd are optional: ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.filesystem] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "<absolute-path-to-your-projects>"] [mcp_servers.context7] command = "npx" args = ["-y", "@upstash/context7-mcp"] startup_timeout_sec = 20 # default is 10 The table name ( filesystem ) is the label you choose. Save the file and restart Codex (in the IDE extension, use Restart extension ). Environment variables and API keys env sets values for the server: env = { API_KEY = "value" } . env_vars lists variable names to allow and forward from your own environment, such as env_vars = ["API_KEY"] , so the secret does not have to sit in the file. Prefer env_vars for real keys, and never commit a config.toml that contains one. A project-level .codex/config.toml is easy to commit by accident. A remote server in config.toml [mcp_servers.example] url = "https://mcp.example.com" bearer_token_env_var = "EXAMPLE_TOKEN" # token read from this variable, sent in Authorization For HTTP servers, url is required. You can add a bearer token from an environment variable ( bearer_token_env_var ), static headers ( http_headers ), or headers read from variables ( env_http_headers ). With none of those, Codex tries stored OAuth credentials, so run codex mcp login <name> for servers that use OAuth. Useful options startup_timeout_sec : seconds to wait for the server to start. Default 10. Raise it if the first npx download is slow. tool_timeout_sec : seconds a tool call may run. Default 60. enabled = false : switch a server off without deleting its config. required = true : make Codex fail at startup if that server cannot initialise. enabled_tools and disabled_tools : allow or deny specific tool names. default_tools_approval_mode : how Codex asks before running the server's tools ( auto , prompt , writes or approve ). OpenAI's configuration reference has the complete list of MCP options. Settings change between Codex releases, so check it for your version. Check that it works Run codex mcp list : the server should appear. Start codex and type /mcp : the server should be listed as active. Ask for something only that server can do, for example "Use the memory server to remember that I prefer tabs", and approve the tool call if asked. Common errors and fixes The server does not appear: check the table is [mcp_servers.<name>] (plural mcp_servers ) and that the TOML is valid. For a project file, the project must be trusted. It times out on the first run: the first npx -y run downloads the package. Raise startup_timeout_sec , or run the command once by hand so it is cached. spawn npx ENOENT , or it fails only on Windows: update Codex, then see Fix "spawn npx ENOENT" on Windows . The server exits at once: run its command yourself in a terminal to see why. Fix MCP error -32000 walks through it. An OAuth server stays unauthenticated: run codex mcp login <name> ; in the desktop app or IDE extension, use Authenticate in the MCP servers list. Using Codex alongside other tools? The same servers can be added to Cursor and Claude Code . More about the agent itself: Codex CLI . FAQ Is the config the same for the CLI and the IDE extension? Yes. OpenAI's docs say the desktop app, CLI and IDE extension share MCP configuration, so you can switch between them without redoing setup. Where do I put an API key? Use env_vars to forward a variable from your shell, or bearer_token_env_var for remote servers, so the key stays out of the file. If you use env or codex mcp add --env , the value is saved in config.toml ; keep that file private. How do I turn a server off without removing it? Set enabled = false in its [mcp_servers.<name>] table. Sources Commands and config above come from these official docs. Tools change often, so check them for the latest steps.
